# How to use this guide

Medicinal Chemistry II continues straight on from Medicinal Chemistry I, and the marks come from the same four places: **classification**, **structure–activity relationship (SAR)**, **mechanism of action with uses**, and the **synthesis of the starred drugs**. The difference is the territory: this paper is mostly cardiovascular, hormonal and anticancer chemistry. Work unit by unit — read the notes, write out the classification table from memory, draw the skeleton and number the SAR points against it, then write each starred synthesis as a numbered scheme without looking. Finish the unit with the question bank and the MCQs.

**How the units here match the syllabus.** The PCI syllabus has five units, and these notes keep one note file per syllabus unit, in the same order. Two things are worth knowing about the split. Unit 1 is the largest, because the syllabus puts antihistamines, anti-ulcer drugs and the whole of cancer chemotherapy into one 10-hour unit; it is written as three clearly separated blocks so you can revise them one at a time. Unit 4 has **no starred drug at all**, so nothing in it needs a synthesis — the marks there are entirely in steroid nomenclature, stereochemistry, SAR and uses.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; learn the full answer with the skeleton, the SAR points and the synthesis where there is one.
- **Medium** — asked every few years, or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for the objective section and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common patterns in pharmacy papers, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Antihistamines, anti-ulcer, anticancer | SAR and classification of H1 blockers, histamine receptors, SAR of H2 blockers, mechanism of proton pump inhibitors, classification of anticancer drugs, alkylating mechanism through the aziridinium ion, methotrexate versus folic acid; synthesis of diphenhydramine, triprolidine, promethazine, cimetidine, mercaptopurine, methotrexate |
| 2 Antianginal, diuretics, antihypertensives | Mechanism of organic nitrates and tolerance, classification of calcium channel blockers, classification of diuretics by site, thiazide SAR, ACE inhibitors, methyldopa as a false transmitter; synthesis of acetazolamide, chlorothiazide, furosemide, methyldopate |
| 3 Antiarrhythmics, lipids, clotting, heart failure | Vaughan Williams classification, cardiac glycoside SAR and digitalis toxicity, statins, bile acid sequestrants, warfarin mechanism with interactions; synthesis of disopyramide and warfarin |
| 4 Endocrine | Steroid nomenclature and stereochemistry, metabolism of steroids, corticosteroid SAR with the prednisolone and dexamethasone changes, oestrogen SAR with diethylstilbestrol, oral contraceptives, thyroid and antithyroid drugs |
| 5 Antidiabetics and local anaesthetics | Classification of oral antidiabetics with mechanisms, sulphonylurea SAR, insulin preparations, **SAR of local anaesthetics** (named in the syllabus), ester versus amide; synthesis of tolbutamide, benzocaine, procaine, dibucaine |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Draw the skeleton first, then number the SAR points against it.** The six that carry the most marks are the H1 antihistamine skeleton, the thiazide nucleus, the steroid nucleus with its numbering, the cardiac glycoside (steroid + lactone + sugar), the sulphonylurea bridge and the three-part local anaesthetic skeleton.
2. **Write syntheses as numbered schemes.** "Reagent → product", with the name of the reaction where it has one (Williamson, Fischer esterification, Michael addition, Strecker, chlorosulphonation, Grignard). Even without neat structures, a correct sequence carries most of the marks.
3. **Classify by mechanism or by site, not by adjectives.** Diuretics are classified by where they act in the nephron; antiarrhythmics by the Vaughan Williams class; anticancer drugs by chemical class. Examiners count the classes and the named examples.
4. **Attach one toxicity tag to each important drug.** Doxorubicin → heart, bleomycin → lung, vincristine → nerves, cisplatin → kidney, amiodarone → thyroid and lung, chlorpropamide → long hypoglycaemia, metformin → lactic acidosis, thioamides → agranulocytosis. These are one-mark gifts in Section A and finish off a Section C answer well.
5. **Two unit-4 traps.** β is up and α is down, and the difference between dexamethasone and betamethasone is only the 16α versus 16β methyl. Say it exactly; do not write "it has a methyl group somewhere".
6. **Do not confuse the look-alike SARs.** Antihistamines need two aryl rings and a tertiary amine; local anaesthetics need one aryl ring, an ester or amide chain and a tertiary amine; sulphonylureas need an aryl ring, the sulphonylurea bridge and an alkyl group. Writing one for another loses the whole question.
7. **Learn the starred drugs cold.** Nineteen drugs carry an asterisk in this syllabus and they are the most likely synthesis questions: diphenhydramine hydrochloride, triprolidine hydrochloride, promethazine hydrochloride, cimetidine, mechlorethamine, mercaptopurine, methotrexate, nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, acetazolamide, chlorothiazide, furosemide, methyldopate hydrochloride, disopyramide phosphate, warfarin, tolbutamide, benzocaine, procaine and dibucaine. Two of these — the organic nitrates — are industrial nitrate esters; for them, learn the **reaction type (esterification of a polyol with nitric acid), the bioactivation to nitric oxide and the SAR**, which is what a written paper can fairly ask. The notes deliberately stop there and give no plant procedure, and the same is true for the nitrogen mustard, where the examinable chemistry is the aziridinium mechanism.
8. **Link chemistry to the clinic in every answer.** Say *why* an ester local anaesthetic causes allergy, *why* an enteric coat is essential for omeprazole, *why* warfarin takes three days to work, *why* benzocaine cannot be injected. One such sentence per answer lifts the grade.
9. **This subject has no practical paper of its own in this semester's scheme**, so everything you learn here is examined in writing. Spend the time you would have spent on experiments on redrawing structures instead.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, learn these six with full skeletons: **SAR of H1 antihistamines**, **thiazide SAR**, **steroid nucleus with numbering and the corticosteroid changes**, **cardiac glycoside SAR**, **sulphonylurea SAR** and **SAR of local anaesthetics**. Then read the synthesis table twice and the toxicity tags once.

## The six skeletons to draw from memory

```text
1. H1 antihistamine   Ar1 ╲
                           X — CH2CH2 — N(CH3)2
                      Ar2 ╱
                      X = O ethanolamine (sedative), N ethylenediamine,
                      C alkylamine (least sedative); amine must be tertiary

2. Thiazide           7-H2NO2S ─[ benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide ]─ 3-substituent
                      6-Cl or 6-CF3 essential; 3,4-dihydro = 10x potency

3. Steroid            rings A-B-C (6) + D (5); C18 on C13, C19 on C10
                      β up (bold), α down (dashed)
                      estrane 18C, androstane 19C, pregnane 21C

4. Cardiac glycoside  sugar(s) — steroid (14β-OH, cis ring fusions) — C17 lactone
                      lactone essential; sugars only change pharmacokinetics

5. Sulphonylurea      Ar(p-substituted) — SO2 — NH — CO — NH — R (3-6 carbons)

6. Local anaesthetic  Ar — [COO ester | NHCO amide] — CH2CH2 — N(C2H5)2
                      base enters the nerve, cation blocks Na+ channel inside
```

## Starred syntheses in one line each

| Drug | Route in one line |
| --- | --- |
| Diphenhydramine | Benzhydrol → benzhydryl chloride → 2-dimethylaminoethanol (Williamson) → HCl salt |
| Triprolidine | 4-Methylphenyl 2-pyridyl ketone → pyrrolidinyl side chain → dehydrate → separate the (E)-isomer |
| Promethazine | Phenothiazine + NaNH2 → 1-dimethylamino-2-chloropropane (branched 3-carbon chain) |
| Cimetidine | 4-Methyl-5-chloromethylimidazole + cysteamine → N-cyano-N',S-dimethylisothiourea |
| Mercaptopurine | Diaminopyrimidinol → formic acid (hypoxanthine) → P2S5 |
| Methotrexate | Tetraaminopyrimidine + dibromopropionaldehyde + p-methylaminobenzoylglutamic acid |
| Nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate | Nitrate **esters**: controlled esterification of the polyol with nitric acid, then diluted and formulated (industrial; learn the reaction type, not a procedure) |
| Acetazolamide | Thiadiazole ring → acetylate the amine → chlorinate the SH to SO2Cl → ammonia |
| Chlorothiazide | m-Chloroaniline + chlorosulphonic acid → ammonia → formic acid ring closure (formaldehyde instead → hydrochlorothiazide) |
| Furosemide | 2,4-Dichlorobenzoic acid → chlorosulphonation → ammonia → furfurylamine |
| Methyldopate | Dimethoxyphenylacetone → Strecker → hydrolyse and demethylate → resolve (S) → esterify with EtOH/HCl |
| Disopyramide | Phenylacetonitrile + 2-chloropyridine → diisopropylaminoethyl chloride → partial hydrolysis to the amide → phosphate |
| Warfarin | 4-Hydroxycoumarin + benzylideneacetone, Michael addition |
| Tolbutamide | p-Toluenesulphonamide + n-butyl isocyanate (base) |
| Benzocaine | p-Nitrotoluene → oxidise → reduce to PABA → Fischer esterification with ethanol |
| Procaine | p-Nitrobenzoic acid → acid chloride → 2-diethylaminoethanol → reduce the nitro group → HCl salt |
| Dibucaine | 2-Hydroxycinchoninic acid → POCl3 → 2-diethylaminoethylamine (amide) → sodium butoxide |

## Mechanisms worth writing in full

```text
Histidine ──(decarboxylase)──► Histamine ; H1 = itch, wheal, bronchospasm
                                            H2 = gastric acid

R—O—NO2 → NO → guanylate cyclase → cGMP ↑ → veins dilate
          (tolerance: keep a nitrate-free interval)

Omeprazole (prodrug) → acid space of parietal cell → sulphenamide
          → S—S bond with H+/K+-ATPase → irreversible block

Nitrogen mustard → aziridinium ion → alkylates guanine N7 → cross-link

Vitamin K cycle ✗ warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase
          → factors II, VII, IX, X not carboxylated (effect after 2–3 days)

Digoxin ✗ Na+/K+-ATPase → Na+ ↑ inside → Ca2+ ↑ → stronger contraction

Sulphonylurea ✗ KATP channel → depolarise → Ca2+ in → insulin released

Local anaesthetic (base in, cation blocks) ✗ voltage-gated Na+ channel
```

## Confusions worth two minutes each

| Pair | How to tell them apart |
| --- | --- |
| Ethanolamine vs alkylamine antihistamine | O bridge = sedative and anticholinergic (diphenhydramine); C bridge = least sedative, most potent (chlorpheniramine) |
| Promethazine vs chlorpromazine | Branched three-carbon chain = antihistamine; straight three-carbon chain = antipsychotic |
| H2 blocker vs proton pump inhibitor | Competitive and reversible at the receptor vs irreversible at the pump |
| Chlorothiazide vs hydrochlorothiazide | 3,4-double bond vs saturated; saturation gives about ten times the potency |
| Loop vs thiazide diuretic | Loop loses calcium, works in renal failure; thiazide keeps calcium, fails at low GFR |
| Spironolactone vs amiloride | Aldosterone receptor antagonist (a steroid) vs direct sodium channel block |
| Nitro compound vs nitrate ester | R—NO2 is inactive here; R—O—NO2 releases nitric oxide |
| Digoxin vs digitoxin | One extra hydroxyl on digoxin: less lipophilic, less protein bound, shorter acting |
| Class IA vs IB antiarrhythmic | IA lengthens the action potential (quinidine), IB shortens it (lidocaine) |
| Cortisone vs hydrocortisone | 11-keto prodrug vs active 11β-hydroxy |
| Dexamethasone vs betamethasone | 16α-methyl vs 16β-methyl epimers |
| T4 vs T3 | Long acting, standard replacement vs fast and brief, for emergencies |
| Ester vs amide local anaesthetic | Plasma esterase, short, allergy through PABA vs liver, longer, rarely allergic |
| Benzocaine vs procaine | No basic amine, surface only vs basic amine, injectable as the hydrochloride |
| Sulphonylurea vs metformin | Releases insulin, causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain vs no insulin release, no hypoglycaemia alone |

## Numbers and facts worth memorising

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Insulin | 51 amino acids, chain A 21 + chain B 30, two interchain disulphides |
| Steroid angular methyls | C18 on C13, C19 on C10 |
| Oestrogen carbons | 18 (aromatic ring A, no C19 methyl) |
| Prednisolone change | Δ1 double bond, about 4 times hydrocortisone |
| Dexamethasone / betamethasone | 9α-fluoro + 16-methyl, about 25–30 times, negligible salt retention |
| Alkylating agents attack | N7 of guanine |
| Warfarin onset | 2–3 days; monitored by INR; antidote vitamin K |
| Nitrate-free interval | 8–12 hours a day to avoid tolerance |
| Thiazide site | Distal convoluted tubule, Na+/Cl- carrier |
| Loop diuretic site | Thick ascending limb, Na+/K+/2Cl- carrier |
| Local anaesthetic blocked first | Small unmyelinated fibres: pain and temperature |
| Digitalis toxicity warning sign | Yellow-green vision; made worse by hypokalaemia |

## Named reactions used in this subject

Williamson ether synthesis (diphenhydramine) · Fischer esterification (benzocaine) · Michael addition (warfarin) · Strecker synthesis (methyldopate) · chlorosulphonation then ammonolysis (chlorothiazide, furosemide, acetazolamide, tolbutamide) · nucleophilic aromatic substitution (furosemide, dibucaine) · Grignard reaction (triprolidine) · partial nitrile hydrolysis to an amide (disopyramide) · aldol condensation (benzylideneacetone for warfarin).

questions.answer:
1. Definition: H1 antihistamines competitively block the H1 receptor, preventing histamine from causing vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, bronchoconstriction and itching.
2. General structure: two aryl rings joined through a connecting atom X to a two-carbon chain ending in a tertiary amine, that is Ar1(Ar2)X-CH2CH2-N(R)2.
3. Classification with examples: (a) Ethanolamines (X = O): diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, doxylamine, clemastine, diphenylpyraline - strongly sedative and anticholinergic. (b) Ethylenediamines (X = N): tripelennamine, antazoline - gastrointestinal upset common. (c) Alkylamines or propylamines (X = C): chlorpheniramine, triprolidine, pheniramine - most potent, least sedative. (d) Piperazines: chlorcyclizine, meclizine, buclizine, cetirizine - long acting, used for vertigo and motion sickness. (e) Phenothiazines: promethazine, trimeprazine - sedative and antiemetic. (f) Tricyclics and miscellaneous: cyproheptadine, azatadine - also block 5-HT and stimulate appetite. (g) Second generation: loratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine, astemizole, fexofenadine - non-sedating. (h) Mast cell stabiliser: cromolyn sodium, which prevents degranulation rather than blocking the receptor.
4. SAR: two aryl rings are needed and should not be coplanar; one ring alone gives weak activity.
5. The connecting atom decides the class and the side-effect pattern: oxygen gives sedation and anticholinergic action, nitrogen gives gastric upset, carbon gives the least sedation with the highest potency.
6. A two-carbon chain between X and the nitrogen is optimum; an alpha-methyl group may improve activity, longer chains reduce it.
7. A tertiary amine is essential; it is protonated at body pH and binds an anionic site on the receptor. Quaternisation removes central effects and lowers activity.
8. Chirality matters in the alkylamines: the (S)-isomer, dexchlorpheniramine, is far more active.
9. A para halogen or small lipophilic group on one ring raises potency and duration.
10. Lipophilicity controls sedation: polar or zwitterionic second-generation drugs such as cetirizine do not enter the brain, so they do not sedate.
11. Uses: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, drug reactions, motion sickness, vertigo, as antiemetics and, for the first generation, as night sedatives. They do not replace adrenaline in anaphylaxis.
questions.question: Classify H1 antihistaminic agents with suitable examples and discuss their structure-activity relationship.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: anticancer drugs act mainly on rapidly dividing cells, so bone marrow depression, mucositis, alopecia, nausea and immunosuppression are shared toxicities.
2. Classification: (a) Alkylating agents - mechlorethamine, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, chlorambucil, busulfan, thiotepa. (b) Antimetabolites - mercaptopurine, thioguanine, fluorouracil, floxuridine, cytarabine, methotrexate, azathioprine. (c) Antibiotics - dactinomycin, daunorubicin, doxorubicin, bleomycin. (d) Plant products - vincristine, vinblastine, etoposide. (e) Miscellaneous - cisplatin, mitotane.
3. Mechanism of alkylating agents: the bis(2-chloroethyl)amino group cyclises internally to a strained three-membered aziridinium (ethyleneimonium) ion, a strong electrophile.
4. This ion attacks the nucleophilic N7 of guanine in DNA; the second arm alkylates another guanine, producing an interstrand cross-link that prevents strand separation and replication.
5. Alkylated guanine also mispairs with thymine and may depurinate, so mutations and strand breaks follow. These drugs are cell cycle non-specific.
6. Structural notes: mechlorethamine is the most reactive and is a vesicant given intravenously; cyclophosphamide is a prodrug activated by liver cytochrome P450 and needs mesna to prevent haemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein; aromatic mustards such as melphalan and chlorambucil are less reactive and orally usable; busulfan is an alkyl disulphonate acting mainly on myeloid cells; thiotepa carries preformed aziridine rings.
7. Mechanism of antimetabolites: they resemble normal metabolites closely enough to be accepted by an enzyme, which is then blocked, or they are incorporated into nucleic acid as a faulty unit. Most are S-phase specific.
8. Folate antagonist: methotrexate differs from folic acid only by a 4-amino group and an N10-methyl group, and inhibits dihydrofolate reductase almost irreversibly, so tetrahydrofolate, thymidylate and purines are not made. Folinic acid rescue protects normal cells.
9. Purine antagonists: mercaptopurine (6-SH instead of 6-OH of hypoxanthine) is converted to thio-IMP and blocks purine synthesis; it is destroyed by xanthine oxidase, so allopurinol raises its toxicity. Azathioprine is its prodrug.
10. Pyrimidine antagonists: fluorouracil becomes FdUMP and blocks thymidylate synthase, causing thymineless death; cytarabine becomes ara-CTP and inhibits DNA polymerase.
11. Uses: leukaemias, lymphomas and solid tumours, usually in combinations that attack different phases and have non-overlapping toxicities.
questions.question: Classify antineoplastic agents with examples. Explain the mechanism of action of alkylating agents and antimetabolites.

questions.answer:
1. Histamine is 2-(4-imidazolyl)ethylamine, formed from histidine by L-histidine decarboxylase and destroyed by diamine oxidase and histamine-N-methyltransferase.
2. Distribution: mast cells of skin, lung and gut; basophils; enterochromaffin-like cells of the stomach; histaminergic neurons of the hypothalamus. Mast cell granules hold it with heparin, and release follows IgE bridging or chemical displacement by morphine or tubocurarine.
3. Receptors: H1 (smooth muscle, endothelium, sensory nerves, brain; Gq) causes bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, oedema, itch and wakefulness; H2 (parietal cell, heart; Gs) causes acid secretion and tachycardia; H3 is a presynaptic autoreceptor in the CNS; H4 is on eosinophils and mast cells in inflammation. The triple response of Lewis demonstrates H1 effects.
4. Development of H2 blockers: starting from histamine itself, the imidazole ring was kept, the side chain was extended to four atoms with a thioether link, and the basic amine was replaced by a neutral, polar, planar group because a charged terminal amine gave agonist activity. Burimamide and metiamide were intermediates; metiamide was withdrawn for agranulocytosis, and replacing its thiourea sulphur with a cyano group gave cimetidine.
5. SAR: a heterocyclic ring (imidazole, furan, thiazole) is needed; a four-atom flexible chain containing sulphur is optimum; the terminal group must be polar, planar and non-basic, such as cyanoguanidine, nitroethenediamine or sulphamoylamidine; a basic group restores agonist activity.
6. Members: cimetidine (imidazole, cyanoguanidine), ranitidine (furan, nitroethenediamine), famotidine (thiazole, sulphamoylamidine, most potent).
7. Mechanism: competitive, reversible blockade of H2 receptors on the parietal cell, which also reduces the response to gastrin and acetylcholine, so basal and nocturnal acid secretion fall.
8. Uses: duodenal and gastric ulcer, reflux disease, stress ulcer prophylaxis, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome as an adjunct.
9. Adverse effects of cimetidine: inhibition of cytochrome P450 with drug interactions, antiandrogenic action causing gynaecomastia and impotence, confusion in the elderly. Ranitidine and famotidine lack these.
10. Proton pump inhibitors: omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole and pantoprazole are benzimidazole-sulphinyl-pyridine prodrugs that concentrate in the acid canaliculus, rearrange to a sulphenamide and form disulphide bonds with the H+/K+-ATPase.
11. Comparison: H2 blockers are competitive and reversible and reduce mainly histamine-driven secretion; proton pump inhibitors block the final common step irreversibly, give greater and longer acid suppression, must be enteric coated and are taken before food.
questions.question: Describe histamine, its receptors and distribution. Discuss the development, SAR and uses of H2 antagonists, and compare them with proton pump inhibitors.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) Benzhydrol (diphenylmethanol) is treated with hydrochloric acid or thionyl chloride to give benzhydryl chloride. (2) The halide is heated with 2-dimethylaminoethanol in the presence of a base, a Williamson ether synthesis, giving 2-(benzhydryloxy)-N,N-dimethylethylamine. (3) Dry hydrogen chloride in an inert solvent precipitates the hydrochloride, which is recrystallised. Combining the base with 8-chlorotheophylline gives dimenhydrinate.
Chemistry: it is an ethanolamine type H1 blocker, so the oxygen bridge gives marked sedation and anticholinergic action.
Uses: allergic rhinitis, urticaria and pruritus, drug and insect-bite reactions, motion sickness and vertigo (as dimenhydrinate), as a night sedative, in cough preparations, and in drug-induced parkinsonism for its central anticholinergic effect.
questions.question: Write the synthesis of diphenhydramine hydrochloride and give its uses.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) 4-Methyl-5-(hydroxymethyl)imidazole is converted with thionyl chloride to 4-methyl-5-(chloromethyl)imidazole hydrochloride. (2) Reaction with cysteamine (2-mercaptoethylamine) lets the thiol displace chloride, giving 2-[(4-methylimidazol-5-yl)methylthio]ethylamine. (3) This amine is condensed with N-cyano-N',S-dimethylisothiourea; methanethiol is eliminated and the cyanoguanidine group is formed, giving cimetidine after crystallisation.
Mechanism: cimetidine is a competitive, reversible antagonist at H2 receptors on the gastric parietal cell. Blocking the receptor prevents histamine from raising cyclic AMP, so the H+/K+-ATPase is less active and acid output falls; the response to gastrin and acetylcholine is also reduced because they partly work through local histamine release. It therefore reduces basal, nocturnal and stimulated acid secretion and is used in peptic ulcer and reflux. Its imidazole ring inhibits cytochrome P450 enzymes, and it has weak antiandrogenic activity.
questions.question: Outline the synthesis of cimetidine and explain its mechanism of action.

questions.answer:
Structure: substituted benzimidazoles joined through a sulphinyl (S=O) bridge to a substituted pyridine ring, for example omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole and pantoprazole.
Mechanism: they are prodrugs and weak bases. They are absorbed, reach the parietal cell through the blood and accumulate selectively in the acidic secretory canaliculus, where the pH is about 1. There they are protonated and rearrange to a reactive cyclic sulphenamide, which forms covalent disulphide bonds with cysteine residues of the H+/K+-ATPase. The pump is irreversibly inhibited, so acid secretion recovers only when new enzyme is synthesised, which takes a day or more, even though the drug itself has a short half-life.
Enteric coating: the drug decomposes rapidly in gastric acid, so an enteric coat is needed to carry it unchanged into the duodenum for absorption.
Before food: the drugs bind only pumps that are actively secreting, so a dose taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, when the greatest number of pumps is working, gives the best inhibition.
Uses: peptic ulcer, reflux disease, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and as part of Helicobacter pylori eradication.
questions.question: Describe the mechanism of action of proton pump inhibitors and explain why they are given as enteric-coated preparations before food.

questions.answer:
Structure: folic acid is a pteridine ring joined through a methylene bridge to p-aminobenzoic acid, which is amide-linked to glutamic acid. Methotrexate differs in only two places: the 4-hydroxy group of the pteridine is replaced by a 4-amino group, and the N10 nitrogen carries a methyl group. It is therefore 4-amino-10-methylfolic acid.
Mechanism: these two changes increase affinity for dihydrofolate reductase about a thousandfold, so the binding is effectively irreversible. Tetrahydrofolate is not regenerated, so the one-carbon transfers that make thymidylate, purines, methionine and serine stop, and DNA synthesis fails. The action is S-phase specific.
Uses: acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, choriocarcinoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, osteosarcoma and breast cancer; in much smaller weekly doses for rheumatoid arthritis and severe psoriasis; and with misoprostol in medical termination under supervision.
Folinic acid rescue: folinic acid (leucovorin) is already a reduced folate, so it does not need dihydrofolate reductase. Given some hours after a high dose of methotrexate, it restores the reduced folate pool of normal marrow and gut cells, which take it up better than tumour cells, and so reduces toxicity without rescuing the tumour.
Toxicity: marrow depression, mucositis, hepatic and renal damage; it must not be given in pregnancy.
questions.question: Compare the structure of methotrexate with folic acid and explain its mechanism, uses and the rationale of folinic acid rescue.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) 4,5-Diamino-6-hydroxypyrimidine is prepared by the standard pyrimidine route from ethyl cyanoacetate and urea, with nitrosation at C5 followed by reduction to the amine. (2) Ring closure of the 4,5-diamine with formic acid builds the imidazole ring and gives hypoxanthine. (3) Heating hypoxanthine with phosphorus pentasulphide in pyridine replaces the 6-oxo group by a thione, giving 6-mercaptopurine, which is isolated as the monohydrate.
Chemistry: it is the thiol analogue of hypoxanthine, a classical antimetabolite.
Mechanism: it is converted by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase to thioinosinic acid, which inhibits the first step of purine synthesis and the conversion of inosinic acid to adenine and guanine nucleotides.
Use: maintenance treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; azathioprine, its prodrug, is used as an immunosuppressant.
Interaction: mercaptopurine is inactivated by xanthine oxidase. Allopurinol inhibits this enzyme, so giving the two together raises mercaptopurine levels sharply and the dose must be reduced substantially to avoid severe marrow depression.
questions.question: Write the synthesis of mercaptopurine and mention its therapeutic use and one important drug interaction.

questions.answer: H1: bronchial and vascular smooth muscle and sensory nerves - bronchoconstriction, vasodilation with oedema and itching. H2: gastric parietal cell and heart - acid secretion and tachycardia. H3: presynaptic nerve endings in the brain - reduced histamine release (autoreceptor). H4: eosinophils, mast cells and bone marrow - chemotaxis in inflammation.
questions.question: Name the histamine receptors with one site and one response for each.

questions.answer: Cyclophosphamide is an inactive cyclic phosphamide prodrug. Liver cytochrome P450 hydroxylates it to 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide, which opens in the cell to phosphoramide mustard, the alkylating species, together with acrolein. Acrolein is excreted in urine and irritates the bladder lining, causing haemorrhagic cystitis. Mesna supplies a free sulphydryl group that traps acrolein in the urine, so the bladder is protected while the anticancer effect is unchanged.
questions.question: Why does cyclophosphamide need to be activated in the liver, and why is mesna given with it?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a diuretic increases urine output by reducing sodium reabsorption in the nephron; water follows sodium osmotically.
2. Classification by site: (a) Proximal tubule - carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: acetazolamide, methazolamide, dichlorphenamide. (b) Proximal tubule and loop - osmotic diuretics: mannitol. (c) Thick ascending limb - loop or high-ceiling diuretics: furosemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid. (d) Distal convoluted tubule - thiazides and related drugs: chlorothiazide, hydrochlorothiazide, hydroflumethiazide, cyclothiazide. (e) Collecting duct - potassium-sparing diuretics: spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist), triamterene and amiloride (sodium channel blockers).
3. Mechanisms in one line each: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors stop the supply of hydrogen ions for Na+/H+ exchange and lose bicarbonate; osmotic diuretics hold water in the tubule; loop diuretics block the Na+/K+/2Cl- carrier; thiazides block the Na+/Cl- carrier; potassium-sparing drugs block the aldosterone receptor or the epithelial sodium channel.
4. Thiazide nucleus: benzothiadiazine-1,1-dioxide, that is a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring containing two nitrogens and a sulphone group.
5. SAR point 1: a free sulphamoyl group (-SO2NH2) at position 7 is essential; substituting its nitrogen abolishes diuretic activity.
6. SAR point 2: an electron-withdrawing group at position 6, usually chlorine or trifluoromethyl, is required; moving it to another position destroys activity.
7. SAR point 3: saturating the 3,4-double bond, as in hydrochlorothiazide, increases potency about tenfold compared with chlorothiazide.
8. SAR point 4: a lipophilic substituent at position 3, as in cyclothiazide, increases potency and prolongs the action.
9. SAR point 5: a small alkyl group on N2 raises lipophilicity and duration; large groups reduce activity.
10. Pharmacological effects: moderate diuresis with loss of sodium, chloride and potassium; reduced urinary calcium; fall in blood pressure, first by volume loss and later by reduced peripheral resistance; a paradoxical antidiuretic effect in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
11. Uses: hypertension, oedema of cardiac, hepatic or renal origin, calcium-containing renal stones, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
12. Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia with gout, hyperglycaemia, raised lipids, and sulphonamide hypersensitivity.
questions.question: Classify diuretics with examples according to their site of action, and discuss the structure-activity relationship of thiazide diuretics.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: blood pressure is the product of cardiac output and peripheral resistance, so drugs act on the heart, the vessels, the kidney or the sympathetic control of all three.
2. Classification: (a) Diuretics - thiazides, furosemide, spironolactone. (b) Beta blockers - timolol, propranolol, atenolol. (c) ACE inhibitors - captopril, enalapril, lisinopril, benazepril, quinapril. (d) Angiotensin receptor blockers - losartan type drugs. (e) Calcium channel blockers - nifedipine, amlodipine, verapamil, diltiazem. (f) Central alpha-2 agonists - clonidine, methyldopa, guanabenz. (g) Adrenergic neuron blockers - guanethidine, reserpine. (h) Direct vasodilators - hydralazine, minoxidil, diazoxide, sodium nitroprusside.
3. The renin-angiotensin system: renin from the kidney converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme, a zinc metallopeptidase, converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, a powerful vasoconstrictor that also releases aldosterone and promotes cardiac remodelling. The same enzyme destroys bradykinin.
4. Mechanism of ACE inhibitors: they occupy the active site of the enzyme, so less angiotensin II is formed; peripheral resistance falls, aldosterone falls with loss of sodium and retention of potassium, and bradykinin, a vasodilator, accumulates.
5. Chemistry: every member carries a group that binds the active-site zinc. Captopril uses a sulphydryl group, enalapril and lisinopril a carboxylate, and fosinopril a phosphinate. A proline or proline-like ring mimics the terminal part of the natural substrate.
6. Prodrugs: enalapril, benazepril and quinapril are ethyl esters hydrolysed in the liver to the active diacids enalaprilat, benazeprilat and quinaprilat. Captopril and lisinopril are active as given.
7. Uses: hypertension of all grades, heart failure, after myocardial infarction, and diabetic nephropathy, where they reduce proteinuria and slow the fall in renal function.
8. Adverse effects: persistent dry cough and rarely angio-oedema, both from accumulated bradykinin; first-dose hypotension; hyperkalaemia; loss of taste and skin rash with captopril, attributed to its thiol group; and renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
9. Contraindications: pregnancy, because the drugs damage the fetal kidney; bilateral renal artery stenosis; and caution with potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium supplements.
10. Comparison: angiotensin receptor blockers act at the receptor, do not raise bradykinin and so do not cause cough, but share the other precautions.
questions.question: Classify antihypertensive agents with examples and discuss the chemistry, mechanism and adverse effects of ACE inhibitors.

questions.answer:
1. Angina is pain arising when the oxygen demand of the myocardium exceeds the coronary supply; drugs act by reducing the work of the heart or improving flow.
2. Chemistry of nitrates: they are esters of nitric acid with a polyhydric alcohol, written R-O-NO2. They are not nitro compounds, in which carbon is bound to nitrogen. The esters are volatile or heat sensitive, so pharmaceutical forms are diluted on an inert carrier such as lactose or made as sublingual tablets, sprays, ointments and patches.
3. Mechanism: in smooth muscle the ester is denitrated, chiefly by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase and tissue thiols, releasing nitric oxide. Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase, cyclic GMP rises, protein kinase G lowers intracellular calcium and dephosphorylates myosin light chain, and the muscle relaxes.
4. Haemodynamic effect: veins dilate more than arteries, so venous return and ventricular filling fall, wall tension and oxygen demand fall, large coronary vessels dilate and collateral flow improves.
5. SAR: the -O-NO2 group is essential; replacing it by -NO2 abolishes activity. Polyols are used so that several ester groups sit on a small framework. More nitrate groups mean greater lipophilicity, potency and instability. Partial denitration in the body gives mono- and dinitrates that remain active and last longer.
6. Members and use: amyl nitrite by inhalation, very brief, also used in cyanide poisoning; nitroglycerin sublingually for an acute attack and by infusion in unstable angina; isosorbide dinitrate orally and sublingually, giving the long-acting 5-mononitrate; pentaerythritol tetranitrate for prophylaxis; dipyridamole, not a nitrate, acts through adenosine and phosphodiesterase and is mainly antiplatelet.
7. Tolerance: continuous exposure depletes tissue thiols and the activating enzyme, so a nitrate-free interval of 8 to 12 hours a day is kept.
8. Adverse effects and interactions: throbbing headache, flushing, postural hypotension and reflex tachycardia; combination with sildenafil-type drugs is contraindicated because both raise cyclic GMP.
9. Calcium channel blockers act on the L-type channel, so less calcium enters cardiac and smooth muscle.
10. Classification: (a) Phenylalkylamines - verapamil, bepridil, acting mainly on the heart. (b) Benzothiazepines - diltiazem, acting on heart and vessels. (c) Dihydropyridines - nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine, nicardipine, nimodipine, acting mainly on vessels; nimodipine is used in cerebral vasospasm.
11. Dihydropyridine SAR: a 1,4-dihydropyridine ring with esters at C3 and C5, methyls at C2 and C6 and an aryl group at C4 held perpendicular to the ring; ortho or meta substitution on that ring is needed, and oxidation of the ring to a pyridine destroys activity, which is why nifedipine is protected from light.
12. Adverse effects: flushing, headache, ankle oedema and reflex tachycardia with dihydropyridines; constipation and bradycardia with verapamil, which must not be combined with a beta blocker.
questions.question: Discuss the chemistry, mechanism of action, SAR and uses of organic nitrates, and classify calcium channel blockers with examples.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) 2,4-Dichlorobenzoic acid is treated with chlorosulphonic acid, which introduces a chlorosulphonyl group at position 5. (2) Treatment with ammonia converts this to a sulphamoyl group, giving 2,4-dichloro-5-sulphamoylbenzoic acid. (3) The chlorine at position 2 is displaced by furfurylamine; the reaction is a nucleophilic aromatic substitution made easy by the electron-withdrawing carboxyl and sulphamoyl groups. The product, 4-chloro-2-(furfurylamino)-5-sulphamoylbenzoic acid, is furosemide.
Mechanism: furosemide inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter on the luminal side of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where about a quarter of filtered sodium is normally reabsorbed. Sodium, potassium and chloride remain in the tubule, the medullary concentration gradient is lost and a large diuresis follows; calcium and magnesium are also lost.
Uses: acute pulmonary oedema, chronic heart failure, oedema of renal or hepatic origin, hypercalcaemia, and forced diuresis in poisoning. It works even when renal function is poor.
Adverse effects: hypokalaemia with alkalosis, hyponatraemia, dehydration and hypotension, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and dose-related ototoxicity after rapid intravenous injection, particularly with aminoglycosides.
questions.question: Write the synthesis of furosemide and explain its mechanism of action and adverse effects.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) m-Chloroaniline is treated with chlorosulphonic acid, which introduces chlorosulphonyl groups at positions 4 and 6 of the ring. (2) Ammonia converts both groups to sulphonamides, giving 4-amino-6-chlorobenzene-1,3-disulphonamide. (3) Ring closure with formic acid joins the aromatic amine and one sulphonamide nitrogen through a one-carbon bridge, giving chlorothiazide. Using formaldehyde in place of formic acid at the last step gives the 3,4-dihydro compound, hydrochlorothiazide.
SAR: (i) a free sulphamoyl group at position 7 is essential and must not be substituted on nitrogen; (ii) an electron-withdrawing group at position 6, chlorine or trifluoromethyl, is required; (iii) saturation of the 3,4-double bond raises potency about tenfold; (iv) a lipophilic group at position 3 increases potency and duration; (v) a small alkyl group on N2 lengthens the action.
Mechanism and use: thiazides block the Na+/Cl- carrier in the distal convoluted tubule, giving a moderate diuresis; they are used in hypertension and in oedema, and they reduce urinary calcium.
questions.question: Write the synthesis of chlorothiazide and give the SAR of thiazide diuretics in brief.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) Thiosemicarbazide is heated with ammonium thiocyanate to build the 2-amino-5-mercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole ring. (2) The amino group is acetylated with acetic anhydride, giving 2-acetamido-5-mercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole. (3) The mercapto group is chlorinated with chlorine in aqueous acid to give the sulphonyl chloride. (4) Treatment with ammonia converts it to the sulphonamide, giving acetazolamide.
Mechanism: carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule cell catalyses the hydration of carbon dioxide to carbonic acid, which supplies the hydrogen ions used in Na+/H+ exchange and so allows bicarbonate and sodium to be reabsorbed. Acetazolamide binds the zinc at the enzyme's active site through its free sulphamoyl group and blocks it, so sodium bicarbonate and water are lost in an alkaline urine.
Limitation: the resulting hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis itself reduces the drug's effect, so diuresis is self-limiting after a few days.
Uses: chronic open-angle and acute glaucoma, because less aqueous humour is formed; acute mountain sickness; some forms of epilepsy; and alkalinisation of urine in the treatment of certain poisonings.
SAR note: a free, unsubstituted sulphonamide group on a heterocyclic ring is essential for activity.
questions.question: Write the synthesis of acetazolamide and explain how carbonic anhydrase inhibitors produce diuresis.

questions.answer:
Mechanism: methyldopa is alpha-methyl-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine, a close analogue of dopa. It is taken up by adrenergic nerve endings and processed by the same enzymes: aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase gives alpha-methyldopamine, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase gives alpha-methylnoradrenaline. This amine is stored and released in place of noradrenaline, hence the name false transmitter. It is a weak agonist at peripheral alpha-1 receptors but a strong agonist at central alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, so sympathetic outflow falls and blood pressure drops with little change in cardiac output or renal blood flow.
Clinical note: it remains a preferred drug for hypertension in pregnancy. Adverse effects include sedation, dry mouth, a positive Coombs test with occasional haemolytic anaemia, drug fever and impaired liver function.
Synthesis of the ester: (1) 3,4-Dimethoxyphenylacetone is subjected to the Strecker reaction with sodium cyanide and ammonium chloride, giving the amino nitrile. (2) Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile and cleavage of the methyl ethers with hydrogen bromide or hydrogen iodide give racemic methyldopa, from which the active (S) or laevo isomer is resolved. (3) Esterification with ethanol saturated with dry hydrogen chloride gives methyldopate hydrochloride, a freely water-soluble salt suitable for intravenous use.
questions.question: Explain methyldopa as a false transmitter and outline the synthesis of methyldopate hydrochloride.

questions.answer:
Potassium-sparing diuretics act in the late distal tubule and collecting duct, where only a small part of sodium is reabsorbed, so their diuretic effect is weak; their value is that they conserve potassium.
1. Spironolactone is a steroid that competes with aldosterone for its cytoplasmic receptor, so the synthesis of sodium channels and pumps is not induced. Its active metabolite canrenone contributes. Uses: heart failure, where it improves survival; resistant hypertension; ascites and oedema of cirrhosis; and primary hyperaldosteronism. Because it is a steroid it causes gynaecomastia, impotence and menstrual irregularity.
2. Triamterene and amiloride are not steroids; they block the epithelial sodium channel directly, so they work whether or not aldosterone is present. They are usually combined with a thiazide to offset potassium loss.
3. The main hazard of all three is hyperkalaemia, which is serious when they are combined with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers or potassium supplements, or used in renal impairment.
Osmotic diuretics: mannitol is a sugar alcohol given by intravenous infusion. It is freely filtered, is not reabsorbed and is pharmacologically inert, so it holds water osmotically within the tubule and increases urine volume. Uses: raised intracranial pressure and cerebral oedema, acute attacks of glaucoma, and maintenance of urine flow in impending acute renal failure or in poisoning. It is contraindicated in established anuria, pulmonary oedema and congestive heart failure, because it first expands the plasma volume.
questions.question: Discuss potassium-sparing diuretics and osmotic diuretics with examples and uses.

questions.answer: Nitrate tolerance is the loss of response that develops within a day of continuous exposure to an organic nitrate, caused mainly by depletion of the tissue thiols and of the mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase needed to release nitric oxide, together with reflex expansion of plasma volume. It is avoided by leaving a daily nitrate-free interval of about 8 to 12 hours, usually overnight, for example by removing a transdermal patch at night or by spacing oral doses asymmetrically.
questions.question: What is nitrate tolerance and how is it avoided?

questions.answer: Sodium nitroprusside releases nitric oxide spontaneously and dilates both arteries and veins, with an effect that begins and ends within minutes, so the blood pressure can be controlled only by a carefully titrated intravenous infusion. The solution decomposes on exposure to light, which both destroys the drug and releases cyanide from its structure, so the container and tubing are shielded and the solution is freshly prepared; prolonged use risks cyanide and thiocyanate accumulation.
questions.question: Why is sodium nitroprusside given only by infusion and protected from light?

questions.answer:
1. The cardiac action potential has five phases: phase 0 the fast upstroke from sodium entry, phase 1 brief repolarisation, phase 2 the plateau held by calcium entry, phase 3 repolarisation by potassium efflux and phase 4 the resting or pacemaker phase.
2. Arrhythmias arise from abnormal automaticity, from triggered activity or from re-entry around a circuit of tissue; drugs act by slowing conduction, lengthening refractoriness or suppressing ectopic pacemakers.
3. Class I - sodium channel blockers, subdivided by their effect on the action potential duration.
4. Class IA - quinidine sulphate, procainamide hydrochloride, disopyramide phosphate: moderate sodium block with added potassium block, so phase 0 is slowed and the action potential and QT interval lengthen. Uses: atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, though now limited by pro-arrhythmia.
5. Class IB - lidocaine hydrochloride, phenytoin sodium, mexiletine, tocainide: weak sodium block with rapid dissociation, acting mainly on depolarised or ischaemic tissue, and shortening the action potential. Uses: ventricular arrhythmias, especially after myocardial infarction; phenytoin for digitalis-induced arrhythmias.
6. Class IC - lorcainide, flecainide, propafenone: strong sodium block that markedly slows conduction with little change in duration. Uses: refractory supraventricular arrhythmias in hearts without structural disease.
7. Class II - beta blockers such as propranolol, esmolol and sotalol: they remove sympathetic drive, slow the sinus node and prolong AV conduction. Uses: rate control in atrial fibrillation, arrhythmias of thyrotoxicosis and exercise, and after myocardial infarction.
8. Class III - amiodarone and sotalol: potassium channel block greatly lengthens the action potential and the refractory period. Uses: serious ventricular arrhythmias and maintenance of sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation.
9. Class IV - calcium channel blockers verapamil and diltiazem: they slow conduction through the AV node. Uses: supraventricular tachycardia and rate control.
10. Unclassified agents: adenosine for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, digoxin for rate control, and magnesium for torsades de pointes.
11. Characteristic toxicities: quinidine causes cinchonism and may lengthen QT; procainamide causes a lupus-like syndrome in slow acetylators; disopyramide is strongly antimuscarinic and depresses contraction; amiodarone affects thyroid, lung, cornea, skin and liver and has a half-life of weeks.
12. General caution: every antiarrhythmic drug can itself cause an arrhythmia, so the indication must be clear and monitoring is essential.
questions.question: Classify antiarrhythmic drugs according to the Vaughan Williams system with examples, and describe the mechanism and uses of each class.

questions.answer:
1. Source and structure: digoxin and digitoxin come from Digitalis species. Each molecule has three parts - a steroid nucleus, an unsaturated five-membered lactone ring at C17 (a cardenolide) and a chain of sugars attached at C3.
2. The steroid nucleus is unusual: rings A/B and C/D are cis fused and there is a 14-beta hydroxyl group, which together give the molecule a characteristic bent shape.
3. SAR point 1: the alpha,beta-unsaturated lactone at C17 is essential; saturating or opening it destroys activity.
4. SAR point 2: the 14-beta hydroxyl and the cis ring junctions are essential; a flat trans-fused molecule is inactive.
5. SAR point 3: the sugars are not needed for the pharmacological action but govern water solubility, absorption, protein binding and duration. Digitoxin has one hydroxyl fewer than digoxin, so it is more lipophilic, better absorbed, far more protein bound and much longer acting, and it is eliminated by the liver whereas digoxin is excreted by the kidney.
6. Mechanism: the glycoside binds the extracellular face of the Na+/K+-ATPase and inhibits it. Intracellular sodium rises, so the sodium-calcium exchanger extrudes less calcium; intracellular calcium rises and more is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, giving a stronger contraction, that is a positive inotropic effect.
7. Electrical effects: increased vagal tone slows the sinus node and prolongs conduction through the atrioventricular node, which is the basis of rate control in atrial fibrillation; at toxic levels automaticity increases and arrhythmias appear.
8. Uses: chronic heart failure with a dilated heart, particularly when atrial fibrillation is present; control of ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation and flutter; and some supraventricular tachycardias.
9. Factors increasing toxicity: hypokalaemia, which is often caused by a diuretic given at the same time, because potassium and the glycoside compete for the same binding site; also hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, hypothyroidism and old age.
10. Features of toxicity: anorexia, nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, confusion, yellow-green visual haloes and blurred vision, and arrhythmias of almost any kind, classically ventricular ectopics with atrioventricular block.
11. Treatment of toxicity: stop the drug and any potassium-losing diuretic, correct potassium, give atropine for bradycardia, phenytoin or lidocaine for ventricular arrhythmia, and digoxin-specific antibody fragments in severe poisoning.
12. Interactions: quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone raise digoxin levels; diuretics raise toxicity through potassium loss.

questions.answer:
1. Haemostasis: the contact and tissue-factor pathways converge on factor X; activated factor X converts prothrombin to thrombin and thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin. Factors II, VII, IX and X require vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation in the liver.
2. Coagulants: menadione (vitamin K3) is a synthetic naphthoquinone, used as its water-soluble bisulphite adduct for injection; acetomenadione is the diacetate of the reduced form, used orally. Uses are bleeding from vitamin K deficiency, haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, obstructive jaundice, malabsorption and reversal of oral anticoagulants. Menadione can cause haemolysis and jaundice in neonates and in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, so phytomenadione is preferred there.
3. Classification of anticoagulants: parenteral (heparin, low molecular weight heparins) and oral (coumarins such as warfarin, and indanediones such as anisindione).
4. Chemistry of warfarin: it is 3-(alpha-acetonylbenzyl)-4-hydroxycoumarin. The flat 4-hydroxycoumarin ring is a bioisostere of the naphthoquinone ring of vitamin K, which is why it competes with the vitamin.
5. Mechanism: warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, so vitamin K is not regenerated from its epoxide and the gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X, and of proteins C and S, fails. The factors produced are inactive.
6. Onset: because factors already in the blood must first be cleared, the effect appears only after two to three days, and warfarin is useless in an emergency; heparin is given first and overlapped.
7. Synthesis: (i) 4-hydroxycoumarin is prepared by cyclisation of a salicylate derivative such as methyl salicylate with ethyl acetate and sodium; (ii) benzylideneacetone is prepared by aldol condensation of benzaldehyde with acetone followed by dehydration; (iii) base-catalysed Michael addition of C3 of 4-hydroxycoumarin to benzylideneacetone gives warfarin, used as the racemate although the (S)-isomer is more potent.
8. Monitoring: prothrombin time expressed as the International Normalised Ratio; the dose is adjusted to the target range for the indication.
9. Antidote: vitamin K, with fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate when bleeding is severe.
10. Interactions: displacement from albumin by aspirin, sulphonamides and phenylbutazone increases the effect; enzyme inhibitors such as cimetidine, metronidazole and fluconazole increase it; enzyme inducers such as rifampicin, phenobarbitone and carbamazepine decrease it; a diet rich in green leafy vegetables decreases it; antiplatelet drugs increase bleeding risk.
11. Contraindication: pregnancy, because warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic; heparin is used instead.
12. Clopidogrel, included with these drugs, is an antiplatelet thienopyridine prodrug activated by cytochrome P450 and irreversibly blocking the platelet P2Y12 receptor for the platelet's lifetime.
questions.question: Discuss coagulants and anticoagulants with special reference to warfarin: its chemistry, mechanism, synthesis, monitoring and interactions.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) 4-Hydroxycoumarin is prepared by cyclising a salicylate derivative, for example methyl salicylate or o-hydroxyacetophenone, with ethyl acetate in the presence of sodium; the C3 position of the product behaves like an active methylene group. (2) Benzylideneacetone (4-phenyl-3-buten-2-one) is prepared by the base-catalysed aldol condensation of benzaldehyde with acetone, followed by loss of water. (3) The two are combined in a base-catalysed Michael addition: C3 of 4-hydroxycoumarin adds to the carbon-carbon double bond of benzylideneacetone, giving warfarin. It is used as the racemate, although the (S)-isomer is several times more active.
Mechanism: the flat 4-hydroxycoumarin ring is a bioisostere of the naphthoquinone ring of vitamin K. Warfarin competitively inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, so reduced vitamin K is not regenerated and the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate the glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX and X. The factors released into the blood cannot bind calcium or phospholipid and are inactive. Because circulating factors must first be used up, the anticoagulant effect appears only after two to three days, and the effect is monitored by the prothrombin time reported as the INR.
questions.question: Write the synthesis of warfarin and explain its mechanism of action.

questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) Phenylacetonitrile is treated with sodium amide and then with 2-chloropyridine; the carbanion displaces the halide to give alpha-phenyl-2-pyridylacetonitrile. (2) A second deprotonation with sodium amide followed by alkylation with 2-(diisopropylamino)ethyl chloride gives 4-(diisopropylamino)-2-phenyl-2-(2-pyridyl)butanenitrile. (3) Partial hydrolysis of the nitrile with concentrated sulphuric acid, stopping at the amide stage, gives disopyramide. (4) Neutralisation with phosphoric acid gives the water-soluble phosphate salt.
Class and mechanism: it is a class IA antiarrhythmic. It blocks the fast sodium channel, slowing phase 0 and conduction, and also blocks potassium channels, which lengthens the action potential and the effective refractory period. This suppresses re-entry and ectopic automaticity.
Uses: ventricular arrhythmias and the maintenance of sinus rhythm after conversion of atrial fibrillation.
Adverse effects: the strongest antimuscarinic action of its class, giving dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and urinary retention; a marked negative inotropic effect, so it is avoided in heart failure; and lengthening of the QT interval with the risk of torsades de pointes.

questions.answer:
Lipoproteins: LDL carries cholesterol to the tissues and is atherogenic, HDL carries it back to the liver and is protective; lowering LDL slows atherosclerosis.
Classification: (1) HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) - lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin. (2) Fibrates - clofibrate, fenofibrate, gemfibrozil. (3) Bile acid sequestrants - cholestyramine, colestipol. (4) Nicotinic acid. (5) Cholesterol absorption inhibitors - ezetimibe.
Statins: lovastatin is a fungal metabolite given as an inactive lactone, which is hydrolysed in the body to the open 3,5-dihydroxy acid. This acid resembles the natural substrate HMG-CoA and competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Falling hepatic cholesterol increases the number of LDL receptors on the liver cell, so plasma LDL is cleared more quickly. Taken at night, when synthesis is highest. Adverse effects: myopathy with raised creatine kinase, rarely rhabdomyolysis, and raised transaminases.
Bile acid sequestrants: these are large insoluble anion-exchange resins that are not absorbed. They bind bile acids in the intestine and prevent their enterohepatic reabsorption, so the liver converts more cholesterol into bile acids and upregulates LDL receptors. They are systemically safe but cause constipation, bloating and an unpleasant texture, and they bind fat-soluble vitamins and other drugs such as digoxin, warfarin and thiazides, which must be taken at least an hour before or several hours after.

questions.answer:
Why it occurs: cardiac glycosides have a narrow margin between a useful and a toxic concentration, and digoxin is excreted by the kidney, so small changes in dose or renal function matter.
Precipitating factors: hypokalaemia, usually caused by a loop or thiazide diuretic given at the same time, because potassium and the glycoside compete for the same site on the Na+/K+-ATPase; also hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, advanced age, hypothyroidism, and drugs that raise digoxin levels such as quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone.
Features: (a) gastrointestinal - anorexia, which is often the first sign, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; (b) central - headache, fatigue, confusion, and in the elderly delirium; (c) visual - blurred vision and the characteristic yellow-green haloes; (d) cardiac - almost any arrhythmia, classically ventricular ectopic beats, bigeminy, atrial tachycardia with block, and varying degrees of atrioventricular block.
Management: stop the glycoside and any potassium-losing diuretic; check and correct serum potassium and magnesium; treat bradycardia and heart block with atropine and, if needed, temporary pacing; treat ventricular arrhythmia with phenytoin or lidocaine; avoid direct current shock if possible; and in severe poisoning give digoxin-specific antibody fragments.

questions.answer:
Background: in heart failure the ventricle cannot maintain output, and the compensatory sympathetic drive and salt and water retention eventually worsen the condition, so unloading the heart is as valuable as strengthening it.
Nesiritide: a recombinant form of human B-type natriuretic peptide, identical with the peptide released by the stretched ventricle. It binds natriuretic peptide receptors, raises cyclic GMP, dilates veins and arteries, lowers filling pressure and promotes sodium and water loss. Being a peptide it is destroyed in the gut, so it is given by intravenous infusion in acutely decompensated heart failure. Hypotension is the main adverse effect.
Bosentan: an orally active non-peptide antagonist at endothelin ETA and ETB receptors. Endothelin-1 is the most powerful endogenous vasoconstrictor and also promotes fibrosis and remodelling, so blocking it lowers pulmonary and systemic vascular resistance. Its established use is pulmonary arterial hypertension. It is hepatotoxic, so liver enzymes are monitored, and it is teratogenic, so pregnancy must be excluded and prevented; it also induces cytochrome P450 enzymes and can reduce the effect of oral contraceptives.
Tezosentan: a short-acting intravenous endothelin receptor antagonist developed for acute decompensated heart failure, used by infusion for its rapid onset and offset.
questions.question: Write a note on nesiritide, bosentan and tezosentan in the management of heart failure.

questions.answer: Procaine is an ester of p-aminobenzoic acid, and esters are rapidly hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterase and by liver esterases, so it is destroyed within minutes and cannot be given by mouth for a systemic effect. Procainamide is the corresponding amide; the amide bond is far more resistant to enzymatic hydrolysis, so the drug survives absorption and the first pass through the liver and is orally active with a useful duration. This is the standard textbook example of the ester-to-amide bioisosteric change made to improve metabolic stability.
questions.question: Why is procainamide orally active while procaine is not?

questions.answer: Amiodarone causes thyroid dysfunction, both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism, because the molecule carries two iodine atoms and releases a large amount of iodine during metabolism; and it causes pulmonary fibrosis with pneumonitis, because the drug is very lipophilic and accumulates in lung tissue over weeks. Corneal microdeposits, slate-grey skin discolouration, hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy occur for the same reason: an extremely long half-life with wide tissue accumulation.
questions.question: Name two organ-specific toxicities of amiodarone and explain why they occur.

questions.answer:
1. The steroid nucleus is cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene: three six-membered rings A, B and C fused as in phenanthrene, with a five-membered ring D.
2. Numbering: carbons 1 to 10 cover rings A and B, 11 to 17 rings C and D; C18 is the angular methyl on C13 and C19 the angular methyl on C10; carbons from C20 onwards make up the side chain at C17.
3. Parent hydrocarbons name the families: estrane with 18 carbons for oestrogens, androstane with 19 carbons for androgens, pregnane with 21 carbons for progestogens and corticosteroids, cholane and cholestane for bile acids and sterols.
4. Stereochemistry: substituents above the plane of the ring system are beta and are drawn with a bold line, those below are alpha and are drawn with a dashed line. The angular methyls are beta in the natural series.
5. Ring fusion: B/C and C/D junctions are trans in almost all active steroids, while the A/B junction may be trans (5-alpha series, a flat extended molecule) or cis (5-beta series, a bent molecule typical of bile acids).
6. The importance of this is biological: 5-alpha-dihydrotestosterone is the potent tissue androgen whereas the 5-beta isomer is almost inactive, and the shape of the whole molecule decides receptor fit.
7. Oestrogens are the exception to the general pattern: ring A is aromatic, so C3 carries a phenolic hydroxyl, and the C19 methyl is absent.
8. Metabolism step 1: reduction of the ring A delta-4-3-ketone by 5-alpha or 5-beta reductase to a 3-hydroxy compound; 5-alpha-reductase is also the activating enzyme for testosterone.
9. Metabolism step 2: interconversion of the 17-keto and 17-beta-hydroxy groups, for example testosterone to androstenedione, by 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase.
10. Metabolism step 3: hydroxylation at C6-beta and C16 by cytochrome P450 enzymes; oestrogens are additionally hydroxylated at C2 and C16 and then methylated by catechol-O-methyltransferase.
11. Metabolism step 4: conjugation of the 3-hydroxy or 17-hydroxy group with glucuronic acid or sulphate to give water-soluble products excreted in urine and bile; 17-ketosteroids in urine are a classical measure of androgen metabolism.
12. Consequences for drug design: natural steroids are destroyed on first pass, so a 17-alpha-alkyl group is introduced to block oxidation at C17 and give oral activity, as in ethinyloestradiol and methyltestosterone; esterification of a 17-beta-hydroxyl with a long-chain acid, as in testosterone enanthate, gives a slowly released depot injection; and cortisone and prednisone are prodrugs that must be reduced at C11 in the liver.
questions.question: Describe the nomenclature and stereochemistry of steroids, and discuss the metabolism of steroids with examples.

questions.answer:
1. The adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids such as cortisol, which control carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism and suppress inflammation, and mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, which control sodium and potassium balance.
2. Classification by potency and duration: short-acting, mainly glucocorticoid with salt-retaining activity - hydrocortisone and cortisone; intermediate-acting - prednisolone, prednisone, methylprednisolone, triamcinolone; long-acting with negligible salt retention - dexamethasone and betamethasone; mainly mineralocorticoid - fludrocortisone and aldosterone.
3. Mechanism: the steroid enters the cell, binds a cytoplasmic receptor, and the complex moves to the nucleus and alters transcription, increasing lipocortin and decreasing cytokines, cyclo-oxygenase-2 and adhesion molecules; the effect therefore takes hours to appear.
4. SAR point 1: the delta-4-3-ketone in ring A is essential for all activity.
5. SAR point 2: an 11-beta-hydroxyl group is essential for glucocorticoid action; the 11-keto compounds cortisone and prednisone are prodrugs reduced in the liver to hydrocortisone and prednisolone.
6. SAR point 3: the C21 hydroxyl of the dihydroxyacetone side chain is essential; esterifying it with succinic or phosphoric acid gives water-soluble injectable forms, and with acetic or acetonide groups gives poorly soluble depot and topical forms.
7. SAR point 4: a 17-alpha-hydroxyl increases glucocorticoid activity.
8. SAR point 5: introducing a 1,2-double bond (delta-1) gives prednisolone, about four times as anti-inflammatory as hydrocortisone with less salt retention.
9. SAR point 6: a 9-alpha-fluorine strongly increases both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, as in fludrocortisone.
10. SAR point 7: a 16-alpha or 16-beta methyl group almost abolishes the salt-retaining action; combined with 9-alpha-fluorine this gives dexamethasone (16-alpha-methyl) and betamethasone (16-beta-methyl), which are about 25 to 30 times as potent as hydrocortisone with negligible sodium retention. A 16-alpha-hydroxyl, as in triamcinolone, acts similarly.
11. Uses: replacement in Addison's disease and secondary adrenal failure; suppression of inflammation in asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and skin disorders; allergic emergencies and anaphylaxis as an adjunct; prevention of transplant rejection; some leukaemias and lymphomas; cerebral oedema; and antenatal use to mature the fetal lung.
12. Adverse effects: Cushingoid appearance with moon face and truncal obesity, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, muscle wasting, thin skin with easy bruising and poor wound healing, peptic ulceration, cataract and glaucoma, susceptibility to infection with masked signs, mood disturbance, growth retardation in children, and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so treatment must be withdrawn gradually.
questions.question: Classify corticosteroids and discuss their structure-activity relationship, uses and adverse effects.

questions.answer:
1. Androgens: testosterone is 17-beta-hydroxyandrost-4-en-3-one, secreted by Leydig cells under luteinising hormone control, converted in target tissue by 5-alpha-reductase to the more potent dihydrotestosterone and by aromatase to oestradiol.
2. Androgen SAR: the delta-4-3-ketone and the 17-beta-hydroxyl are needed for full activity; a 17-alpha-alkyl group blocks first-pass metabolism and gives oral activity, as in methyltestosterone; esterifying the 17-beta-hydroxyl gives depot injections such as testosterone propionate and enanthate; removing the C19 methyl, as in nandrolone, shifts the balance towards anabolic and away from androgenic action.
3. Androgen uses and harms: replacement in male hypogonadism and delayed puberty, and anabolic use in wasting states; misuse in sport causes liver damage, adverse lipid changes, suppression of natural hormone production, infertility and virilisation in women.
4. Oestrogens: oestradiol is the most potent natural hormone, with oestrone and oestriol as weaker metabolites, oestriol being characteristic of pregnancy. Chemically they are unique in having an aromatic ring A with a phenolic 3-hydroxyl and no C19 methyl, so they belong to the estrane series with 18 carbons.
5. Oestrogen SAR: the pharmacophore is a phenolic hydroxyl at one end and a hydroxyl or ketone at the other, separated by a fixed distance of about 10.9 angstrom on a rigid lipophilic framework; 17-alpha-ethinylation blocks metabolism and gives the orally active ethinyloestradiol, whose 3-methyl ether mestranol is a prodrug.
6. Non-steroidal oestrogen: diethylstilbestrol is a stilbene carrying two phenolic rings. Only the trans isomer is active, because it places the two oxygens at the required distance; the cis isomer is much weaker. Its use in pregnancy caused genital tract cancers in daughters and is of historical importance only.
7. Progestogens: progesterone is pregn-4-ene-3,20-dione; it prepares the endometrium, quietens the uterus and raises basal body temperature, but is destroyed rapidly by mouth. Synthetic analogues are either 19-nor compounds derived from testosterone, such as norethisterone, norgestrel and levonorgestrel, or 17-alpha-acetoxyprogesterones such as medroxyprogesterone acetate.
8. Oral contraceptives: combined preparations contain an oestrogen, usually ethinyloestradiol, with a progestogen such as levonorgestrel or norgestrel; progestogen-only preparations contain the progestogen alone.
9. Mechanism: steady hormone levels suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary axis so that the mid-cycle surge of luteinising hormone does not occur and ovulation is prevented; the progestogen also thickens cervical mucus so that sperm cannot penetrate and renders the endometrium unsuitable for implantation.
10. Adverse effects: nausea, breast tenderness, weight gain, breakthrough bleeding, raised blood pressure, and an increased risk of venous thromboembolism that is much greater in smokers over 35. Enzyme-inducing drugs such as rifampicin, phenytoin and carbamazepine can cause failure.
11. Benefits: reliable contraception, regular and lighter periods, less dysmenorrhoea, and reduced risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer.
12. Mifepristone is a progesterone receptor antagonist, also a glucocorticoid antagonist, used under medical supervision for medical termination of early pregnancy within the limits of the law; it is a prescription-only drug in India and is not available over the counter.
questions.question: Discuss sex hormones and oral contraceptives: their chemistry, SAR, mechanism and adverse effects.

questions.answer:
The parent compound is hydrocortisone (cortisol), a pregnane with a delta-4-3-ketone, 11-beta, 17-alpha and 21-hydroxyl groups and a C20 ketone.
1. The delta-4-3-ketone in ring A is essential for all activity.
2. An 11-beta-hydroxyl is essential for glucocorticoid action; 11-keto compounds such as cortisone and prednisone are prodrugs reduced in the liver.
3. The C21 hydroxyl is essential; its esters control solubility - sodium succinate and sodium phosphate for injection, acetate and acetonide for depot and topical use.
4. A 17-alpha-hydroxyl raises glucocorticoid potency.
5. A 1,2-double bond gives prednisolone, about four times as potent an anti-inflammatory as hydrocortisone with less sodium retention.
6. A 9-alpha-fluorine raises both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid potency strongly, as in fludrocortisone, which is used for mineralocorticoid replacement.
7. A 16-alpha or 16-beta methyl, or a 16-alpha-hydroxyl, almost abolishes mineralocorticoid activity. With 9-alpha-fluorine this gives dexamethasone (16-alpha-methyl) and betamethasone (16-beta-methyl), about 25 to 30 times as potent with negligible salt retention, and triamcinolone (16-alpha-hydroxyl).
8. 6-alpha-methyl or 6-alpha-fluoro substitution increases potency further, as in methylprednisolone.
