questions.answer:
Synthesis of thyroid hormone: the gland traps iodide by an active pump, thyroid peroxidase oxidises it and iodinates tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin to give mono- and di-iodotyrosine, and the coupling of these residues forms thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which are released by proteolysis. In the tissues 5'-deiodinase converts T4 to T3, the active hormone.
Thyroid drugs: L-thyroxine (levothyroxine) is the standard replacement in hypothyroidism because its long half-life gives steady blood levels and it is converted to T3 in the tissues; it is taken on an empty stomach and the dose is adjusted by measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone. L-thyronine (liothyronine) acts within hours and lasts briefly, and is reserved for myxoedema coma. Only the laevo isomers are active; the molecule is two iodinated phenyl rings joined by an ether oxygen with an alanine side chain.
Antithyroid drugs: propylthiouracil and methimazole are thioamides that inhibit thyroid peroxidase, so iodide is not organified and hormone is not made; propylthiouracil also blocks the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, which is useful in thyroid storm. Because stored hormone must be used up first, improvement takes several weeks.
Adverse effects: rash, arthralgia and gastrointestinal upset; agranulocytosis is the serious reaction, so fever or sore throat must be investigated immediately; propylthiouracil can cause severe liver injury.
Other measures: iodide in large amounts briefly blocks hormone release and firms the gland before surgery, radioactive iodine-131 ablates thyroid tissue, and beta blockers control tremor, tachycardia and anxiety while the thioamides take effect.
questions.question: Write a note on thyroid and antithyroid drugs.

questions.answer:
Physiology: sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide from nerve endings and endothelium in the corpus cavernosum. Nitric oxide activates guanylate cyclase, cyclic GMP rises, intracellular calcium falls, the smooth muscle of the arterioles and trabeculae relaxes, blood fills the sinusoids and the outflow veins are compressed, producing an erection. Cyclic GMP is then destroyed by phosphodiesterase type 5.
Mechanism of the drugs: sildenafil and tadalafil are selective inhibitors of phosphodiesterase type 5, so cyclic GMP is not broken down and the natural response is amplified and prolonged. They do not themselves initiate an erection; sexual stimulation is still needed.
Chemistry: sildenafil is a pyrazolopyrimidinone that mimics the purine ring of cyclic GMP, and tadalafil is a beta-carboline with a longer duration of action.
Other uses: sildenafil and tadalafil are also used in pulmonary arterial hypertension, where the same mechanism relaxes pulmonary vessels.
Adverse effects: headache, flushing, nasal congestion, dyspepsia and, with sildenafil, a transient blue tinge to vision from weak inhibition of phosphodiesterase type 6 in the retina.
Contraindication: concurrent use of any organic nitrate, because nitrates raise cyclic GMP by producing nitric oxide and the inhibitor prevents its breakdown; the combination can cause a severe and prolonged fall in blood pressure. Caution is also needed in unstable cardiovascular disease.
questions.question: Explain the mechanism of action of drugs used in erectile dysfunction and state their important contraindication.

questions.answer:
Natural oestrogens: oestradiol, oestrone and oestriol are steroids of the estrane series with 18 carbons. They differ from all other steroids in two ways - ring A is aromatic, so C3 carries a phenolic hydroxyl, and the C19 angular methyl group is absent. Oestradiol has a 17-beta-hydroxyl and is the most potent; oestrone has a 17-ketone; oestriol has an additional 16-alpha-hydroxyl and is the weakest, and is the main oestrogen of pregnancy.
SAR: (1) the aromatic ring A with its phenolic 3-hydroxyl is essential and acts as a hydrogen-bond donor at the receptor; (2) a hydroxyl or ketone at the far end of a rigid lipophilic framework, about 10.9 angstrom from the phenolic oxygen, completes the pharmacophore; (3) a 17-beta configuration of the hydroxyl is required, the 17-alpha isomer being much weaker; (4) 17-alpha-ethinylation blocks oxidation at C17 and gives the orally active ethinyloestradiol, whose 3-methyl ether mestranol is a prodrug; (5) esterification of the 3- or 17-hydroxyl gives longer-acting injectable forms.
Diethylstilbestrol: a non-steroidal stilbene bearing two phenolic rings. Only the trans isomer is active, because it holds the two phenolic oxygens at approximately the distance found in oestradiol, while the cis isomer brings them too close; this is the standard example of geometrical isomerism matching a pharmacophore. It is no longer used in pregnancy, since exposure in utero caused genital tract cancers in daughters.
Uses of oestrogens: hormone replacement at the menopause, primary ovarian failure, and contraception in combination with a progestogen.
questions.question: Describe the chemistry and SAR of oestrogens, including diethylstilbestrol.

questions.answer:
Androgens: testosterone, 17-beta-hydroxyandrost-4-en-3-one, is the principal male hormone, secreted by the Leydig cells of the testis under the control of luteinising hormone. In target tissues 5-alpha-reductase converts it to dihydrotestosterone, which binds the androgen receptor more strongly, and aromatase converts part of it to oestradiol.
SAR: (1) the delta-4-3-ketone in ring A and the 17-beta-hydroxyl group are needed for full activity; (2) a 17-alpha-methyl or ethyl group prevents oxidation of the 17-hydroxyl and gives oral activity, as in methyltestosterone and oxymetholone, but also causes cholestatic liver injury; (3) esterification of the 17-beta-hydroxyl with propionic, enanthic or decanoic acid gives oily depot injections releasing drug over days or weeks; (4) removal of the C19 angular methyl, giving the 19-nor series such as nandrolone, favours anabolic over androgenic activity; (5) ring A modifications such as the 2-oxa group of oxandrolone also raise the anabolic to androgenic ratio.
Therapeutic uses: replacement in male hypogonadism, delayed puberty and after orchidectomy; hereditary angio-oedema; and anabolic use in severe wasting and some anaemias.
Misuse: anabolic steroids are misused to increase muscle bulk and performance. Harms include liver damage and tumours with 17-alpha-alkyl drugs, a fall in HDL cholesterol with cardiovascular risk, suppression of natural testosterone production with testicular atrophy and infertility, acne, aggression and mood change, virilisation and menstrual disturbance in women, and premature closure of the epiphyses in adolescents. Their use is prohibited in sport and they are prescription-only drugs.
questions.question: Write a note on androgens and anabolic steroids with their SAR and misuse.

questions.answer:
Dexamethasone and betamethasone are epimers that differ only in the configuration of the methyl group at C16: dexamethasone carries a 16-alpha-methyl and betamethasone a 16-beta-methyl group. Both also carry a 9-alpha-fluorine and a delta-1 double bond, both are about 25 to 30 times as potent an anti-inflammatory as hydrocortisone, and both have negligible salt-retaining activity.
Cortisone differs from hydrocortisone in having an 11-keto group instead of an 11-beta-hydroxyl. Since the 11-beta-hydroxyl is essential for glucocorticoid action, cortisone is a prodrug that must be reduced in the liver to hydrocortisone, so it is ineffective when applied topically and unreliable in liver disease.
questions.question: Differentiate between dexamethasone and betamethasone, and between cortisone and hydrocortisone.

questions.answer: In the conventional drawing of a steroid the ring system lies in the plane of the paper. A substituent pointing above that plane, towards the viewer, is said to be beta and is drawn with a bold or solid line; a substituent pointing below the plane, away from the viewer, is alpha and is drawn with a broken or dashed line. The two angular methyl groups C18 and C19 are beta in natural steroids, and the same convention describes ring fusions, for example the 5-alpha (trans, flat) and 5-beta (cis, bent) series.
questions.question: What is meant by the alpha and beta orientation of substituents in steroids?

questions.answer:
1. Background: type 2 diabetes combines resistance to insulin with a failing beta cell, so drugs either make more insulin available, make the tissues more sensitive, or slow the entry of glucose from the gut.
2. Classification: (a) Sulphonylureas - tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, glipizide, glibenclamide, glimepiride. (b) Biguanides - metformin. (c) Thiazolidinediones - pioglitazone, rosiglitazone. (d) Meglitinides - repaglinide, nateglinide. (e) Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors - acarbose, voglibose. (Newer classes outside the syllabus list include DPP-4 inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors.)
3. Sulphonylureas: they bind the SUR1 subunit of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel of the beta cell; the channel closes, the membrane depolarises, calcium enters and stored insulin is released. They therefore need surviving beta cells and are useless in type 1 diabetes. First-generation drugs are tolbutamide and chlorpropamide; second-generation drugs carry a large arylcarboxamidoethyl group and are about a hundred times more potent.
4. Sulphonylurea adverse effects: hypoglycaemia, which may be prolonged with chlorpropamide and in the elderly; weight gain; nausea; rash; and with chlorpropamide a disulfiram-like flush with alcohol and dilutional hyponatraemia.
5. Biguanides: metformin activates AMP-activated protein kinase, reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis, improves insulin sensitivity in muscle and slightly reduces appetite. It does not release insulin, so by itself it does not cause hypoglycaemia and does not cause weight gain; it is the first-choice drug in type 2 diabetes, especially with obesity.
6. Metformin adverse effects: metallic taste, nausea and diarrhoea at the start of treatment, reduced vitamin B12 absorption on long use, and the rare but serious lactic acidosis, so it is avoided in renal impairment, severe liver disease, poor tissue perfusion and alcoholism, and is withheld around contrast radiography and major surgery.
7. Thiazolidinediones: they bind the nuclear receptor PPAR-gamma, chiefly in fat cells, and alter the transcription of genes controlling insulin sensitivity; the effect takes several weeks. They are insulin sensitisers and do not cause hypoglycaemia alone. Adverse effects: fluid retention and oedema, weight gain, precipitation of heart failure and fractures in women; liver function is monitored because an earlier member was withdrawn for hepatotoxicity.
8. Meglitinides: repaglinide and nateglinide close the same potassium channel at a different binding site but act and disappear quickly, so they are taken just before each meal to control the rise in glucose after eating and suit irregular meal times. They can cause brief hypoglycaemia.
9. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: acarbose and voglibose competitively inhibit the brush border enzymes that split disaccharides and oligosaccharides, so carbohydrate is absorbed more slowly and the peak after meals is blunted. They act within the gut and are barely absorbed.
10. Their adverse effects follow directly: flatulence, abdominal discomfort and diarrhoea from unabsorbed carbohydrate fermented in the colon. If hypoglycaemia occurs because another drug is also being taken, it must be treated with glucose, not with sucrose, which cannot be split while the enzyme is inhibited.
11. Choice in practice: metformin first unless contraindicated, with a sulphonylurea, a glitazone or another class added when control is inadequate, and insulin when the beta cell fails.
12. General measures remain essential: diet, weight reduction, exercise, and control of blood pressure and lipids to prevent complications.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a local anaesthetic reversibly blocks impulse conduction along nerve fibres in a restricted area without loss of consciousness.
2. General structure: a lipophilic aromatic portion, an intermediate chain containing an ester or amide link, and a hydrophilic portion that is usually a tertiary amine.
3. Classification by chemistry: (a) Benzoic acid derivatives - cocaine, hexylcaine, meprylcaine, cyclomethycaine, piperocaine. (b) Amino benzoic acid esters - benzocaine, butamben, procaine, butacaine, propoxycaine, tetracaine, benoxinate. (c) Anilides or amides - lignocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, etidocaine. (d) Miscellaneous - phenacaine, diperodon, dibucaine.
4. Mechanism: the drug is a weak base with a pKa around 8 to 9. The unionised free base crosses the nerve membrane; inside the axon the ionised cation binds a receptor at the inner mouth of the voltage-gated sodium channel, preferring the open and inactivated states.
5. Consequence: sodium entry is blocked, the threshold for excitation rises, the rate of rise of the action potential falls, conduction slows and finally fails.
6. Fibre susceptibility: small unmyelinated fibres are blocked first, so pain and temperature are lost before touch, pressure and motor power; the use-dependent block means rapidly firing fibres are affected most.
7. SAR point 1: all three parts of the molecule are needed; losing the aromatic ring destroys potency and losing the amine removes water solubility and the ability to make a salt.
8. SAR point 2: the aromatic ring supplies lipophilicity, which determines potency and duration; a para-amino or para-alkoxy group raises electron density on the carbonyl and increases potency, and long alkyl or alkoxy chains, as in tetracaine and dibucaine, raise both potency and toxicity.
9. SAR point 3: the linkage decides metabolism. Esters are hydrolysed quickly by plasma pseudocholinesterase and are short acting, and their p-aminobenzoic acid metabolite causes allergy; amides are metabolised slowly in the liver, last longer and seldom cause allergy.
10. SAR point 4: an intermediate chain of two to three atoms is optimum; branching near the carbonyl or the nitrogen slows metabolism and lengthens action, as in mepivacaine and etidocaine.
11. SAR point 5: the amine should be tertiary with a pKa near physiological pH so that enough free base exists outside to cross the membrane and enough cation exists inside to block the channel; quaternary compounds cannot penetrate from outside. Benzocaine is the exception, having no basic amine and being used only on surfaces.
12. Clinical consequences and uses: inflamed acidic tissue gives a poor block because little free base is present; adrenaline added to the solution prolongs the block and reduces systemic absorption, but is never used in fingers, toes, ears, nose or penis. Routes are surface application, infiltration, nerve block, spinal and epidural anaesthesia and intravenous regional anaesthesia. Systemic toxicity begins with perioral numbness, metallic taste, light-headedness and tinnitus, and progresses to twitching, convulsions and depression of respiration and the heart.

1. Insulin is a protein hormone of 51 amino acids in two chains, chain A of 21 and chain B of 30 residues, joined by two interchain disulphide bridges with a third bridge inside chain A.
2. It is synthesised as proinsulin, from which the connecting C-peptide is removed before secretion; measuring C-peptide therefore shows how much insulin the patient's own pancreas produces.
3. Actions: it increases glucose uptake into muscle and fat through the GLUT4 transporter, promotes glycogen, protein and fat synthesis, and inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and lipolysis.
4. Because it is a protein it is destroyed by gastric and intestinal enzymes and must be injected subcutaneously, or given intravenously in emergencies.
5. Sources: formerly extracted from pig and beef pancreas, now almost entirely human insulin produced by recombinant technology, or analogues in which amino acids have been changed to alter absorption.
6. Preparations: rapid-acting analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) do not form hexamers and act within minutes; regular soluble insulin is short acting and the only form given intravenously; isophane or NPH insulin is complexed with protamine to give intermediate action; long-acting analogues glargine, which precipitates at tissue pH, and detemir, which binds albumin through a fatty acid chain, give a flat profile; premixed preparations combine short and intermediate forms.
7. Uses: all type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes when oral drugs fail or are contraindicated, diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar states, during pregnancy, surgery and serious infection, and in hyperkalaemia with glucose.
8. Adverse effects: hypoglycaemia is the chief hazard, with sweating, tremor, palpitation, confusion and coma, treated with oral glucose, intravenous dextrose or glucagon; also local lipodystrophy, weight gain, and allergy, which is now rare.
9. Sulphonylureas: the common skeleton is an arylsulphonylurea, Ar-SO2-NH-CO-NH-R. Members are tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, glipizide, glibenclamide and glimepiride.
10. Mechanism: they close the ATP-sensitive potassium channel on the beta cell by binding its SUR1 subunit, so the cell depolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels open and stored insulin is released.
11. SAR: the sulphonylurea bridge is essential and a thiourea is less active; the aryl ring needs a para substituent, small in the first generation (methyl in tolbutamide, chlorine in chlorpropamide) and a bulky arylcarboxamidoethyl group in the second generation, which raises potency about a hundredfold; the substituent on the terminal nitrogen should be an alkyl or cycloalkyl group of about three to six carbons, a cyclohexyl ring giving a long action; and duration follows metabolism, so tolbutamide, whose para methyl group is readily oxidised, is short acting while chlorpropamide, with an unoxidisable chlorine, acts for more than a day.
12. Synthesis of tolbutamide: toluene is treated with chlorosulphonic acid to give p-toluenesulphonyl chloride, which ammonia converts to p-toluenesulphonamide; the sulphonamide is then treated with a base and with n-butyl isocyanate, and the sulphonamide nitrogen adds across the isocyanate to give the sulphonylurea, which is recovered on acidification and recrystallised.

Synthesis: (1) p-Nitrotoluene is oxidised with potassium dichromate and sulphuric acid, or with potassium permanganate, to p-nitrobenzoic acid. (2) The acid is converted to its acid chloride with thionyl chloride. (3) The acid chloride is esterified with 2-diethylaminoethanol in the presence of a base, giving 2-diethylaminoethyl p-nitrobenzoate. (4) The aromatic nitro group is reduced with iron and hydrochloric acid, or by catalytic hydrogenation, to give the aromatic amine, that is procaine. (5) Dry hydrogen chloride in an inert solvent precipitates procaine hydrochloride, a freely water-soluble salt. An alternative route esterifies p-aminobenzoic acid directly with 2-diethylaminoethanol.
Chemistry: it is the 2-diethylaminoethyl ester of p-aminobenzoic acid, the classical ester type local anaesthetic.
Uses: infiltration anaesthesia and nerve block for minor surgery and dental work, usually with adrenaline to prolong the effect; as procaine penicillin, where salt formation gives a long-acting depot injection. It is not effective as a surface anaesthetic because it penetrates mucous membranes poorly.
Drawbacks: short duration because plasma pseudocholinesterase hydrolyses it quickly, and hypersensitivity caused by its p-aminobenzoic acid metabolite; a patient allergic to it can be given an amide such as lignocaine.

Synthesis: (1) p-Nitrotoluene is oxidised with potassium dichromate and sulphuric acid, or with alkaline potassium permanganate, to p-nitrobenzoic acid. (2) The nitro group is reduced with tin or iron and hydrochloric acid, or by catalytic hydrogenation, giving p-aminobenzoic acid. (3) Fischer esterification with excess ethanol and a small amount of concentrated sulphuric acid under reflux gives ethyl p-aminobenzoate; the mixture is poured into water, neutralised with sodium carbonate, and the solid is filtered and recrystallised from dilute ethanol. The melting point of the pure product is about 90 degrees Celsius.
Why surface use only: benzocaine has an aromatic ring and an ester link but no basic aliphatic amine, so it cannot be protonated and cannot form a water-soluble salt suitable for injection. It is almost insoluble in water, so it stays where it is applied and is absorbed slowly, and its action depends on the unionised molecule entering the nerve endings directly beneath the surface.
Uses: creams, gels, lozenges, sprays and dusting powders for painful mouth and throat conditions, for ulcers, and on wounds, burns and haemorrhoids.
Caution: excessive application, particularly in infants, has been associated with methaemoglobinaemia.

Synthesis: (1) Toluene is treated with chlorosulphonic acid, which gives p-toluenesulphonyl chloride. (2) Treatment with ammonia converts the sulphonyl chloride to p-toluenesulphonamide. (3) The sulphonamide is deprotonated with a base such as sodium hydroxide or sodium methoxide and treated with n-butyl isocyanate; the sulphonamide nitrogen adds across the isocyanate carbon-nitrogen double bond to form the sulphonylurea. (4) Acidification precipitates tolbutamide, which is recrystallised. An alternative route condenses p-toluenesulphonamide with n-butylamine through a urethane or carbamate intermediate.
Mechanism: sulphonylureas bind the SUR1 subunit of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in the membrane of the pancreatic beta cell. The channel closes, so potassium cannot leave; the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels open, intracellular calcium rises and insulin-containing granules are released by exocytosis. The effect is independent of blood glucose, which is why hypoglycaemia can occur. Long-term treatment also appears to reduce hepatic insulin clearance and improve tissue sensitivity. Because stored insulin is required, these drugs are ineffective in type 1 diabetes and in advanced beta cell failure.
Note on tolbutamide: its para methyl group is readily oxidised in the liver, so it is short acting and comparatively safe in the elderly.

Synthesis of dibucaine (cinchocaine): (1) 2-Hydroxycinchoninic acid, that is 2-hydroxyquinoline-4-carboxylic acid, is the starting material. (2) Treatment with phosphorus oxychloride or phosphorus pentachloride converts the 2-hydroxyl to a chlorine and the carboxyl group to an acid chloride, giving 2-chloroquinoline-4-carbonyl chloride. (3) Reaction with 2-diethylaminoethylamine forms the carboxamide at position 4. (4) Heating with sodium n-butoxide displaces the chlorine at position 2 by a butoxy group, giving dibucaine, which is converted to the hydrochloride for solutions. It is the most potent and most toxic of the group and is used mainly for surface and spinal anaesthesia.
Comparison:
(1) Chemistry: esters carry a -COO- link, amides an -NHCO- link.
(2) Metabolism: esters are hydrolysed rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterase and tissue esterases; amides are metabolised slowly by liver microsomal enzymes, so their effect is prolonged in liver disease.
(3) Duration: esters are generally short acting, amides longer acting.
(4) Allergy: esters yield p-aminobenzoic acid, a recognised allergen, so hypersensitivity is relatively common; amides rarely cause allergy, and a patient sensitive to an ester can be given an amide.
(5) Stability: amide solutions are more stable to heat and can be autoclaved, whereas ester solutions hydrolyse on storage.
(6) Examples: esters - cocaine, procaine, benzocaine, tetracaine; amides - lignocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, etidocaine, dibucaine.

Metformin: a biguanide, a small very polar molecule. It activates AMP-activated protein kinase in the liver and muscle, which reduces gluconeogenesis and hepatic glucose output, increases glucose uptake and use by muscle, reduces fatty acid oxidation and slightly reduces appetite and intestinal glucose absorption. It does not stimulate insulin release, so used alone it does not cause hypoglycaemia and it does not cause weight gain; some insulin must nevertheless be present for it to work. It is the first-choice drug in type 2 diabetes, especially in overweight patients, and is also used in polycystic ovary syndrome.
Adverse effects of metformin: metallic taste, anorexia, nausea and diarrhoea, which usually settle if the dose is increased slowly; impaired vitamin B12 absorption on long use; and the rare but potentially fatal lactic acidosis. It is therefore avoided in renal impairment, severe hepatic disease, heart failure with poor perfusion, hypoxic states and alcoholism, and is withheld before procedures using iodinated contrast media and before major surgery.
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: acarbose and voglibose are carbohydrate-like molecules that competitively inhibit the alpha-glucosidase enzymes of the intestinal brush border, so disaccharides and oligosaccharides are split more slowly and glucose enters the blood gradually. The peak after a meal is reduced. They act locally and are hardly absorbed, so they do not cause hypoglycaemia alone, and they must be taken with the first mouthful of food.
Adverse effects: flatulence, abdominal cramps, borborygmi and diarrhoea, from carbohydrate fermented by colonic bacteria; rarely raised liver enzymes. Important practical point: if a patient on one of these drugs together with a sulphonylurea or insulin becomes hypoglycaemic, glucose must be given, since sucrose cannot be hydrolysed while the enzyme is inhibited.

questions.answer: Inflamed tissue is acidic. A local anaesthetic is a weak base, so in an acidic environment most of it exists as the ionised cation, which cannot cross the lipid nerve membrane; too little free base penetrates to the axon and the block is poor. Adrenaline is added because it constricts local blood vessels, so the drug is removed more slowly from the site. This keeps a higher concentration at the nerve, prolongs the block, reduces bleeding in the operative field and lowers the peak blood level and thus systemic toxicity. It must not be used in areas supplied by end arteries such as fingers, toes, ears, nose and penis.

questions.answer: Regular soluble insulin molecules associate into zinc-containing hexamers in the vial and in the subcutaneous depot, and these must dissociate into monomers before absorption, which delays the onset by about half an hour. In rapid-acting analogues a few amino acids near the end of the B chain are exchanged or reversed, for example the proline and lysine at B28 and B29 in insulin lispro, which weakens the forces holding the hexamer together. The analogue therefore dissociates at once, is absorbed within minutes and can be injected immediately before or even just after a meal, giving better control of the rise in glucose after eating and a lower risk of late hypoglycaemia.

# Unit 1: Antihistaminic agents, anti-ulcer drugs and antineoplastic agents

Three blocks sit in this unit. First the **H1 antihistamines**, second the **H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors** that reduce gastric acid, third the **antineoplastic (anticancer) agents**. Starred drugs in the syllabus are diphenhydramine hydrochloride, triprolidine hydrochloride, promethazine hydrochloride, cimetidine, mechlorethamine, mercaptopurine and methotrexate. For the anticancer alkylating agents the examinable chemistry is the **alkylation mechanism**, not a laboratory preparation, and that is what these notes cover.

## 1.1 Histamine, its receptors and their distribution

Histamine is **2-(4-imidazolyl)ethylamine**: an imidazole ring carrying a two-carbon chain that ends in a primary amine. It is formed in the body by decarboxylation of the amino acid **histidine** (enzyme: L-histidine decarboxylase, cofactor pyridoxal phosphate) and is destroyed by **diamine oxidase (histaminase)** and by **histamine-N-methyltransferase**.

Storage sites: mast cells of skin, lung and gut; basophils; the enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells of the stomach wall; and histaminergic neurons of the hypothalamus. Mast cell granules hold it bound to heparin. Release follows antigen bridging of IgE on the mast cell surface (type I hypersensitivity) or direct displacement by chemicals such as tubocurarine, morphine and radiocontrast media.

| Receptor | Main site | Effect when stimulated | Transduction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H1 | Bronchial and gut smooth muscle, capillary endothelium, sensory nerves, brain | Bronchoconstriction, vasodilation with oedema and itch, wakefulness | Gq → IP3 / DAG, calcium rises |
| H2 | Gastric parietal cell, heart, uterus | Acid secretion, tachycardia | Gs → cAMP rises |
| H3 | Presynaptic in the CNS | Less histamine release (autoreceptor) | Gi |
| H4 | Eosinophils, mast cells, bone marrow | Chemotaxis in inflammation | Gi |

The **triple response of Lewis** (red spot → flare → wheal) after an intradermal injection is the classical demonstration of H1 vasodilation, axon-reflex flare and capillary leak.

## 1.2 H1 antihistamines: general structure and SAR

Almost every classical H1 blocker fits one skeleton:

```text
   Ar1 ╲
        X — CH2 — CH2 — N(R)2      X = O (ethanolamines)
   Ar2 ╱                            X = N (ethylenediamines)
                                    X = CH (propylamines / alkylamines)
                                    Ar1–Ar2 joined by S and N = phenothiazines
                                    Ar–CH–N in a ring = piperazines, tricyclics
```

SAR points examiners ask for:

1. **Two aryl rings** (phenyl, substituted phenyl, pyridyl, thienyl) are needed for good potency; one ring alone gives weak activity. The rings must not be coplanar — a slight twist fits the receptor best.
2. **The connecting atom X** sorts the drugs into chemical classes and decides the side effects: oxygen (ethanolamines) gives strong sedation and marked anticholinergic action; nitrogen (ethylenediamines) gives more gastrointestinal upset; carbon (alkylamines) gives the least sedation and the highest potency.
3. **A two-carbon chain** between X and the nitrogen is optimal; lengthening or branching reduces activity, except for a methyl on the alpha carbon, which can improve it.
4. **A tertiary amine** is essential. It is protonated at body pH, and the cation binds an anionic site on the receptor. Primary, secondary or quaternary nitrogen lowers activity; quaternisation also removes central effects.
5. **Chirality.** In the propylamines the (S)-isomer is far more active (dexchlorpheniramine is the active enantiomer of chlorpheniramine); in the ethanolamines the two isomers differ little.
6. **Halogen or small lipophilic substituent para on one ring** (chlorpheniramine, chlorcyclizine) raises potency and duration.
7. **Lipophilicity decides sedation.** Second-generation drugs are more polar or carry a carboxylic acid (cetirizine) or are P-glycoprotein substrates, so they stay out of the brain.

## 1.3 Classification of H1 antihistamines with uses

| Chemical class | Examples | Notes and uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ethanolamines | Diphenhydramine*, dimenhydrinate, doxylamine succinate, clemastine fumarate, diphenylpyraline | Strongly sedative and anticholinergic; motion sickness, allergy, insomnia, antiparkinsonian use of diphenhydramine |
| Ethylenediamines | Tripelennamine, antazoline | Moderately sedative, gastric upset common |
| Alkylamines (propylamines) | Chlorpheniramine maleate, triprolidine*, pheniramine | Least sedative of the first generation, highly potent, used by day |
| Piperazines | Chlorcyclizine, meclizine, buclizine, cetirizine, levocetirizine | Long acting; meclizine and buclizine for vertigo and motion sickness |
| Phenothiazines | Promethazine*, trimeprazine | Sedative, antiemetic, antipruritic; promethazine also used in anaphylaxis as an adjunct |
| Tricyclics / miscellaneous | Cyproheptadine, azatadine | Cyproheptadine also blocks 5-HT and stimulates appetite |
| Second generation | Astemizole, loratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine | Non-sedating, once daily; astemizole and terfenadine were withdrawn for QT prolongation |
| Mast cell stabiliser | Cromolyn sodium (sodium cromoglycate) | Not a receptor blocker; it prevents mast cell degranulation and is used prophylactically in asthma and allergic rhinitis |

**Common uses:** allergic rhinitis, urticaria and pruritus, drug and insect-bite reactions, motion sickness and vertigo, as antiemetics, in cough mixtures, and (first generation only) as night sedatives. They relieve the symptoms of anaphylaxis but never replace adrenaline.

### Synthesis of diphenhydramine hydrochloride

1. **Benzhydrol** (diphenylmethanol) is treated with hydrochloric acid or thionyl chloride to give **benzhydryl chloride**.
2. The halide is heated with **2-dimethylaminoethanol** with a base to take up the hydrogen chloride; a Williamson ether synthesis gives 2-(benzhydryloxy)-N,N-dimethylethylamine.
3. Treatment with hydrogen chloride in dry solvent gives the **hydrochloride salt**. (Combining this base with 8-chlorotheophylline gives **dimenhydrinate**.)

### Synthesis of triprolidine hydrochloride

1. **4-Methylacetophenone** is condensed with **2-pyridinecarbaldehyde**-derived intermediates in the usual route; practically, 1-(4-methylphenyl)-1-(2-pyridyl) ketone is first made by reacting 2-cyanopyridine with the Grignard reagent from 4-bromotoluene, then hydrolysing.
2. The ketone reacts with the Grignard reagent or the carbanion from **1-(2-chloroethyl)pyrrolidine**/pyrrolidine-containing fragment to give the tertiary alcohol.
3. **Dehydration** with acid gives the propenylamine; the desired geometry is the **(E)-isomer**, which is separated and converted to the hydrochloride.

### Synthesis of promethazine hydrochloride

1. **Phenothiazine** is treated with **sodium amide** (or sodium hydride) in an inert solvent to give the sodium salt at the ring nitrogen.
2. The salt is alkylated with **1-dimethylamino-2-chloropropane**, giving the branched three-carbon side chain that distinguishes promethazine from the antipsychotic phenothiazines.
3. The base is converted to the **hydrochloride**. Remember the rule: a **two-carbon branched chain (isopropyl type) gives an antihistamine**, a straight **three-carbon chain gives an antipsychotic**.

## 1.4 H2 antagonists

Blocking H2 receptors on the parietal cell stops histamine-driven acid secretion and reduces the response to gastrin and acetylcholine as well. They are used in peptic ulcer, gastro-oesophageal reflux and stress ulcer prophylaxis.

**SAR in brief.** Cimetidine came from histamine itself: an imidazole ring was kept, the side chain was lengthened to four atoms with a **thioether** in it, and the basic amino group was replaced by a **neutral, polar, planar guanidine-type group (cyanoguanidine)**, because a charged amine gave agonist activity. Later drugs replaced the imidazole by **furan (ranitidine)** or **thiazole (famotidine)** and used nitro-ethenediamine or sulphamoylamidine end groups; these are more potent and lack cimetidine's antiandrogenic effect and its inhibition of cytochrome P450.

| Drug | Ring | Polar end group | Point to remember |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cimetidine* | Imidazole | Cyanoguanidine | Inhibits CYP enzymes, gynaecomastia on long use |
| Ranitidine | Furan with dimethylaminomethyl | Nitroethenediamine | More potent, fewer interactions |
| Famotidine | Thiazole with guanidine | Sulphamoylamidine | Most potent of the three |

### Synthesis of cimetidine

1. **4-Methyl-5-(chloromethyl)imidazole hydrochloride** (obtained from the hydroxymethyl compound with thionyl chloride) is reacted with **cysteamine (2-mercaptoethylamine)**; the thiol displaces chloride to give 2-[(4-methylimidazol-5-yl)methylthio]ethylamine.
2. This amine is treated with **N-cyano-N',S-dimethylisothiourea** (made from dimethyl cyanodithioimidocarbonate and methylamine); methanethiol is lost and the cyanoguanidine is formed.
3. The product is crystallised to give **cimetidine**.

## 1.5 Gastric proton pump inhibitors

Omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole and pantoprazole are **substituted benzimidazoles linked by a sulphinyl (S=O) bridge to a pyridine ring**. They are prodrugs.

```text
Benzimidazole — S(=O) — CH2 — pyridine(substituted)
        │ accumulates in the acid space of the parietal cell (pH ~1)
        │ protonated, then rearranges
   active sulphenamide (cyclic, cationic)
        │ forms S—S bonds with cysteine residues
   H+/K+-ATPase irreversibly inhibited
```

Points for the exam: they are weak bases that concentrate only in the secretory canaliculus, so action is selective; they must be given as **enteric-coated** forms because they decompose in stomach acid; inhibition is **irreversible**, so acid output returns only when new pump protein is made (which is why a short half-life still gives a long effect); best taken before a meal, when pumps are active. Uses: peptic and duodenal ulcer, reflux disease, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and with antibiotics for *Helicobacter pylori*.

## 1.6 Antineoplastic agents

Cancer chemotherapy attacks dividing cells, so the main toxicities are shared: bone marrow depression, mucositis, hair loss, nausea and vomiting, infertility and immunosuppression.

### Classification

| Class | Members in the syllabus | Mechanism in one line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alkylating agents | Mechlorethamine*, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, chlorambucil, busulfan, thiotepa | Attach alkyl groups to DNA bases (mainly N7 of guanine), cross-link the strands |
| Antimetabolites | Mercaptopurine*, thioguanine, fluorouracil, floxuridine, cytarabine, methotrexate*, azathioprine | Fake building blocks that block nucleotide synthesis |
| Antibiotics | Dactinomycin, daunorubicin, doxorubicin, bleomycin | Intercalate DNA, inhibit topoisomerase II, make free radicals |
| Plant products | Etoposide, vinblastine sulphate, vincristine sulphate | Act on the mitotic spindle or topoisomerase II |
| Miscellaneous | Cisplatin, mitotane | Platinum cross-links DNA; mitotane is adrenolytic |

### Alkylating agents

The nitrogen mustards carry a **bis(2-chloroethyl)amino group**. In the body the nitrogen lone pair displaces one chloride internally to form a strained three-membered **aziridinium (ethyleneimonium) ion**, a powerful electrophile. This ion alkylates the **N7 of guanine**; the second arm then alkylates another guanine, giving an **interstrand cross-link** that stops replication. Alkylated guanine also mispairs with thymine and depurinates. Because they do not need the cell to be in a particular phase, alkylating agents are **cell cycle non-specific**.

Structural differences that matter:

- **Mechlorethamine** is the most reactive and must be given intravenously into a running drip; it is a vesicant.
- **Cyclophosphamide** is a cyclic phosphamide **prodrug**, inactive until hydroxylated by liver cytochrome P450 to 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide, which opens to phosphoramide mustard (active) and acrolein (bladder toxin). **Mesna** is given with it to trap acrolein and prevent haemorrhagic cystitis.
- **Melphalan** (phenylalanine mustard) and **chlorambucil** carry an aromatic ring, which lowers the nitrogen's basicity and makes them stable enough for oral use.
- **Busulfan** is an alkyl disulphonate (methanesulphonate ester); it acts mainly on myeloid cells and is used in chronic myeloid leukaemia; pulmonary fibrosis is its typical late toxicity.
- **Thiotepa** contains three aziridine rings already formed.

### Antimetabolites

| Drug | Resembles | Mechanism | Main use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mercaptopurine* | Hypoxanthine (6-SH replaces 6-OH) | Converted to thio-IMP, blocks purine synthesis; inactivated by xanthine oxidase, so allopurinol raises its levels | Acute leukaemia |
| Thioguanine | Guanine | Same family as above | Acute leukaemia |
| Azathioprine | Prodrug of mercaptopurine | Immunosuppression | Transplants, autoimmune disease |
| Fluorouracil | Uracil (5-F) | FdUMP blocks thymidylate synthase, so DNA lacks thymine ("thymineless death") | Solid tumours, topical in skin cancers |
| Floxuridine | Deoxyuridine analogue | Converted to the same active nucleotide | Infused in liver tumours |
| Cytarabine | Deoxycytidine with arabinose sugar | Ara-CTP inhibits DNA polymerase and is incorporated into DNA; S-phase specific | Acute myeloid leukaemia |
| Methotrexate* | Folic acid | Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so no tetrahydrofolate, no thymidylate or purines | Leukaemia, choriocarcinoma; also rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis in small weekly doses |

**Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue** restores reduced folate to normal cells after high-dose methotrexate. Methotrexate differs from folic acid in two ways only: an **amino group replaces the 4-hydroxy** of the pteridine, and the **N10 carries a methyl group**; these two changes raise its affinity for dihydrofolate reductase about a thousandfold and make the binding effectively irreversible.

### Synthesis of mercaptopurine

1. **4,5-Diaminopyrimidin-6-ol (4,5-diamino-6-hydroxypyrimidine)** is prepared from ethyl cyanoacetate and thiourea or urea by the standard pyrimidine route, followed by nitrosation at C5 and reduction to the amine.
2. Ring closure of the diamine with **formic acid** builds the imidazole ring, giving **hypoxanthine**.
3. Heating hypoxanthine with **phosphorus pentasulphide** in pyridine replaces the 6-oxo group with a thione, giving **6-mercaptopurine**, isolated as the monohydrate.

### Synthesis of methotrexate

1. **2,4,5,6-Tetraaminopyrimidine** (or its 2,4-diamino-6-hydroxy precursor) is the pteridine building block.
2. It is condensed with **2,3-dibromopropionaldehyde** (a three-carbon unit) together with **p-methylaminobenzoyl-L-glutamic acid**. The reaction builds the pyrazine ring of the pteridine and joins it through a methylene bridge to the N-methyl-p-aminobenzoyl glutamate fragment in one pot.
3. The crude product is purified by dissolving in alkali and reprecipitating at acid pH, giving **methotrexate** (4-amino-10-methylfolic acid).

### Antibiotics, plant products and miscellaneous agents

- **Dactinomycin (actinomycin D)** inserts between G-C pairs and blocks RNA polymerase; used in Wilms' tumour.
- **Daunorubicin and doxorubicin** are anthracyclines: they intercalate, poison topoisomerase II and generate free radicals; their special toxicity is **dose-related cardiomyopathy**.
- **Bleomycin** chelates iron, makes oxygen radicals and cuts DNA strands; marrow sparing, but causes **pulmonary fibrosis**.
- **Vincristine and vinblastine** bind tubulin and stop spindle formation (metaphase arrest); vincristine's limiting toxicity is **neuropathy**, vinblastine's is marrow depression.
- **Etoposide**, from podophyllotoxin, inhibits topoisomerase II and arrests cells in late S / G2.
- **Cisplatin** loses its chloride ligands inside the cell and forms intrastrand cross-links with adjacent guanines, acting much like an alkylating agent; it is highly emetic and **nephrotoxic**, so hydration and amifostine are used.
- **Mitotane**, related to the insecticide DDT, destroys adrenal cortical cells and is used in adrenal carcinoma.

## Remember

1. Histamine = imidazole + two-carbon chain + primary amine, made from histidine; H1 causes itch, wheal and bronchoconstriction, H2 causes acid secretion.
2. H1 blocker skeleton: two aryl rings → X (O, N or C) → two carbons → tertiary amine. X decides the class and the side effects; the amine must be tertiary.
3. Alkylamines are the least sedating first-generation drugs; ethanolamines the most sedating; second-generation drugs stay out of the brain.
4. Promethazine's branched three-carbon side chain makes it an antihistamine, not an antipsychotic.
5. Cimetidine kept histamine's imidazole but replaced the basic amine with a neutral cyanoguanidine; ranitidine uses furan, famotidine thiazole.
6. Proton pump inhibitors are acid-activated prodrugs that irreversibly block H+/K+-ATPase; give enteric coated, before food.
7. Nitrogen mustards act through an aziridinium ion that cross-links guanine N7; cyclophosphamide is a liver-activated prodrug and needs mesna.
8. Methotrexate = folic acid with 4-NH2 and N10-CH3; it blocks dihydrofolate reductase and is rescued by folinic acid.
9. Toxicity tags worth one mark each: doxorubicin → heart, bleomycin → lung, vincristine → nerves, cisplatin → kidney, busulfan → lung fibrosis, cyclophosphamide → bladder.

# Unit 2: Antianginal drugs, diuretics and antihypertensive agents

This unit covers three groups that all act on the circulation: drugs that relieve **angina** (organic nitrates and calcium channel blockers), **diuretics** classified by their site in the nephron, and **antihypertensive agents**. Starred drugs are nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, acetazolamide, chlorothiazide, furosemide and methyldopate hydrochloride. For the two organic nitrates the examinable chemistry is their **chemical nature, bioactivation and SAR**; nitrate esters are manufactured under strict industrial control and diluted before use, so no preparation procedure is given here.

## 2.1 Angina and the organic nitrates

Angina is chest pain from a mismatch between the oxygen the heart muscle needs and what the coronary flow supplies. Drugs help by lowering the work of the heart (preload and afterload), by widening coronary vessels, or by slowing the rate.

**Chemistry.** The organic nitrates are **esters of nitric acid with an alcohol (R—O—NO2)**. They are not nitro compounds (R—NO2) — a favourite one-mark question. The more nitrate ester groups the molecule has, the more lipophilic and the more potent it is, but the shorter the shelf life; they decompose with heat and shock, so pharmaceutical forms are **diluted on lactose or a similar carrier**, or formulated as sublingual tablets, sprays, ointments and transdermal patches.

**Mechanism of action.**

```text
R—O—NO2  ──(mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase, thiols)──►  NO (nitric oxide)
                 │
      activates soluble guanylate cyclase in smooth muscle
                 │
           GTP ──► cyclic GMP rises
                 │
   protein kinase G: less intracellular Ca2+, myosin light chain dephosphorylated
                 │
             VASODILATION (veins >> arteries)
```

Venodilation lowers venous return, so the ventricle is less stretched and needs less oxygen. Large coronary arteries also dilate and collateral flow improves. **Tolerance** develops within a day of continuous exposure (depletion of tissue thiols and of the activating enzyme), so a **nitrate-free interval** of 8–12 hours each day is part of the treatment. Sublingual use avoids the heavy first-pass metabolism that destroys an oral dose. Nitrates must never be combined with sildenafil-type drugs, because both raise cGMP and the fall in pressure can be severe.

| Drug | Form used | Point to remember |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amyl nitrite | Inhaled vapour, volatile ester | Very quick, very brief; also used in cyanide poisoning to form methaemoglobin |
| Nitroglycerin* (glyceryl trinitrate) | Sublingual tablet, spray, patch, infusion | The standard for an acute attack; tablets lose potency on storage |
| Isosorbide dinitrate* | Sublingual and oral | Active metabolite isosorbide 5-mononitrate gives a longer action |
| Pentaerythritol tetranitrate | Oral | Long acting, used for prophylaxis |
| Dipyridamole | Oral | Not a nitrate: inhibits adenosine uptake and phosphodiesterase; mainly an antiplatelet drug, can cause coronary steal |

**SAR of organic nitrates in brief.** Activity needs the **—O—NO2 ester group**; replacing it by —NO2 abolishes it. Polyol esters (glycerol, isosorbide, pentaerythritol) are used because a polyol gives several ester groups on a small framework. Increasing the number of nitrate groups raises lipophilicity, potency and the risk of decomposition; partial denitration in the body yields mono- and dinitrates that are still active but more water soluble and longer lasting.

**Manufacture, in general terms.** Both starred nitrates are nitrate esters made industrially by the controlled esterification of the parent alcohol (glycerol; isosorbide) with nitrating acid, then carefully washed, neutralised and immediately diluted or formulated. In an exam answer state the reaction type (**esterification of a polyol with nitric acid**), the product and the need for dilution and stabilisation — the plant procedure itself is not an exam requirement and is not reproduced here.

## 2.2 Calcium channel blockers

These block the **L-type voltage-gated calcium channel**, so less calcium enters cardiac and smooth muscle. The result is vasodilation, less force of cardiac contraction and, for some, slowing of the SA and AV nodes.

| Chemical class | Drugs | Where they act most | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phenylalkylamines | Verapamil, bepridil hydrochloride | Heart (rate and conduction) | Angina, supraventricular arrhythmia, hypertension |
| Benzothiazepines | Diltiazem hydrochloride | Heart and vessels equally | Angina, hypertension |
| Dihydropyridines | Nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine, nicardipine, nimodipine | Vessels (little cardiac effect) | Hypertension, angina; nimodipine for cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage |

SAR of the dihydropyridines: a **1,4-dihydropyridine ring** with ester groups at C3 and C5, a methyl at C2 and C6 and an **aryl group at C4** that must be roughly perpendicular to the ring. *Ortho* or *meta* substitution on that aryl ring (nitro in nifedipine) gives high activity; *para* substitution lowers it. Oxidation of the ring to a pyridine destroys activity, which is why nifedipine must be protected from light. Different esters change duration: amlodipine's basic side chain gives a very long half-life and once-daily dosing.

Dihydropyridines can cause reflex tachycardia, flushing, headache and ankle oedema; verapamil causes constipation and must not be combined with a beta blocker because both depress the AV node.

## 2.3 Diuretics

A diuretic increases urine volume by reducing sodium reabsorption; water follows the sodium. Classify them by their site in the nephron.

```text
 Glomerulus
    │
 Proximal tubule ──────────── carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide)
    │                         osmotic diuretics act here and in the loop (mannitol)
 Descending limb
 Thick ascending limb ─────── loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid)
    │                         Na+/K+/2Cl- carrier
 Distal convoluted tubule ─── thiazides (chlorothiazide, hydrochlorothiazide)
    │                         Na+/Cl- carrier
 Collecting duct ──────────── potassium-sparing (spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride)
```

### Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

Acetazolamide, methazolamide and dichlorphenamide are **sulphonamides with an unsubstituted —SO2NH2 group**, which is essential: it binds the zinc at the active site of carbonic anhydrase. Blocking the enzyme stops the supply of hydrogen ions for Na+/H+ exchange, so sodium bicarbonate and water are lost. The urine turns alkaline and the blood develops a **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis**, which is also why the drug becomes less effective after a few days (self-limiting).

SAR: a **heterocyclic ring carrying a free sulphamoyl group**; substitution on the sulphonamide nitrogen abolishes activity; an acyl group on the ring amino (acetazolamide) improves pharmacokinetics.

Uses: glaucoma (less aqueous humour), acute mountain sickness, certain epilepsies, and to alkalinise urine.

**Synthesis of acetazolamide.** 1. **Thiosemicarbazide** is heated with **ammonium thiocyanate** to build the 2-amino-5-mercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole ring. 2. The amino group is acetylated with **acetic anhydride**. 3. The mercapto group is **chlorinated with chlorine in aqueous acid** to give the sulphonyl chloride. 4. Treatment with **ammonia** converts it to the sulphonamide, giving acetazolamide.

### Thiazides and related drugs

Chlorothiazide, hydrochlorothiazide, hydroflumethiazide and cyclothiazide share the **benzothiadiazine-1,1-dioxide** nucleus. They block the Na+/Cl- co-transporter in the distal tubule.

```text
            Cl (or CF3) at 6
              │
   H2NO2S ──[ benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide ]── position 3 substituent
   at position 7                                 2,3-dihydro = more potent
```

SAR points:

1. A **free sulphamoyl group at position 7** is essential for activity.
2. An **electron-withdrawing group at position 6** (chlorine, trifluoromethyl) is needed; moving it to position 7 destroys activity.
3. **Saturating the 3,4-double bond** (hydrochlorothiazide versus chlorothiazide) raises potency about ten times.
4. A **lipophilic substituent at position 3** (as in cyclothiazide) increases potency and duration.
5. Substitution on N2 with a small alkyl group increases lipophilicity and duration.

Effects and uses: moderate diuresis, lower blood pressure (initially by volume loss, later by reduced peripheral resistance), reduced urinary calcium (so useful in calcium stones) and a paradoxical benefit in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Unwanted effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia and raised lipids.

**Synthesis of chlorothiazide.** 1. **m-Chloroaniline** (3-chloroaniline) is treated with **chlorosulphonic acid**, which puts two chlorosulphonyl groups on the ring at positions 4 and 6. 2. Treatment with **ammonia** converts both to sulphonamides, giving 4-amino-6-chlorobenzene-1,3-disulphonamide. 3. Ring closure with **formic acid** (or formamide) joins the aromatic amine and one sulphonamide nitrogen through a one-carbon bridge, giving **chlorothiazide**. (Using formaldehyde instead of formic acid at step 3 gives the 3,4-dihydro compound, **hydrochlorothiazide**.)

### Loop (high-ceiling) diuretics

Furosemide, bumetanide and ethacrynic acid block the **Na+/K+/2Cl- carrier in the thick ascending limb**, where about a quarter of filtered sodium is reabsorbed — hence the large, rapid diuresis. They also lose calcium and magnesium in the urine and can cause hypokalaemic alkalosis, dehydration and, in high intravenous doses, **ototoxicity**.

Uses: acute pulmonary oedema and heart failure, oedema of renal or hepatic origin, hypercalcaemia, and forced diuresis in poisoning.

SAR: furosemide is an **anthranilic acid (5-sulphamoyl-2-aminobenzoic acid) derivative** — it needs a free carboxylic acid, a sulphamoyl group and a lipophilic substituent on the nitrogen (furfuryl in furosemide, phenoxy in bumetanide). Ethacrynic acid is chemically different: an **aryloxyacetic acid with an α,β-unsaturated ketone** that binds sulphydryl groups, so it works where sulphonamides fail.

**Synthesis of furosemide.** 1. **2,4-Dichlorobenzoic acid** is treated with **chlorosulphonic acid** to introduce a chlorosulphonyl group at position 5. 2. Reaction with **ammonia** gives the 5-sulphamoyl compound. 3. The chlorine at position 2 is displaced by **furfurylamine** (nucleophilic aromatic substitution, helped by the electron-withdrawing groups), giving **4-chloro-2-(furfurylamino)-5-sulphamoylbenzoic acid**, that is furosemide.

### Potassium-sparing diuretics and osmotic diuretics

- **Spironolactone** is a steroid that competes with aldosterone at its cytoplasmic receptor in the collecting duct; it spares potassium, is used in heart failure, resistant hypertension, ascites of cirrhosis and primary hyperaldosteronism, and causes gynaecomastia because of its steroid nucleus. Its metabolite canrenone is also active.
- **Triamterene and amiloride** are not steroids; they block the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) directly, so they work whether or not aldosterone is present.
- All three carry a real risk of **hyperkalaemia**, especially with ACE inhibitors or potassium supplements.
- **Mannitol** is a sugar alcohol given intravenously; it is filtered, not reabsorbed, and holds water in the tubule by osmosis. Uses: raised intracranial pressure, acute glaucoma, and to maintain urine flow in impending renal failure. It must not be used in established anuria or pulmonary oedema, because it first expands the plasma volume.

## 2.4 Antihypertensive agents

Blood pressure is cardiac output multiplied by peripheral resistance, so a drug can act on the heart, the vessels, the kidney or the nervous control of all three.

| Group | Drugs in the syllabus | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Beta blocker | Timolol | Blocks β1: less output, less renin; also used as eye drops in glaucoma |
| ACE inhibitors | Captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, benazepril hydrochloride, quinapril hydrochloride | Block the conversion of angiotensin I to II and slow the breakdown of bradykinin |
| Central α2 agonists | Clonidine hydrochloride, methyldopate hydrochloride*, guanabenz acetate | Stimulate α2 receptors in the brainstem, reducing sympathetic outflow |
| Adrenergic neuron blocker | Guanethidine monosulphate | Enters the nerve ending and prevents noradrenaline release |
| Vasodilators | Hydralazine hydrochloride, minoxidil, diazoxide, sodium nitroprusside | Relax arterioles directly; nitroprusside releases nitric oxide and dilates both sides |
| Rauwolfia alkaloid | Reserpine | Empties vesicular stores of amines |

Notes worth marks:

- **ACE inhibitors** all carry a zinc-binding group: a **sulphydryl in captopril**, a **carboxylate in enalapril and lisinopril**, a **phosphinate in fosinopril**. Captopril's thiol explains its rash and taste disturbance. Most of the others are **ester prodrugs** (enalapril → enalaprilat; quinapril → quinaprilat). The **dry cough** and the rare angio-oedema come from accumulated bradykinin. They are contraindicated in pregnancy and in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
- **Methyldopa** is itself a prodrug: it is decarboxylated and hydroxylated in the nerve ending to **α-methylnoradrenaline**, a false transmitter that is a strong α2 agonist, so central sympathetic outflow falls. It is still the preferred drug in **hypertension of pregnancy**. **Methyldopate hydrochloride** is its ethyl ester, made water soluble for injection. Side effects include sedation, a positive Coombs test and haemolytic anaemia, and drug fever.
- **Clonidine** is an imidazoline α2 agonist; sudden withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.
- **Sodium nitroprusside** is given only by infusion, protected from light, and its cyanide-containing structure limits the duration of use.
- **Minoxidil and diazoxide** open potassium channels; minoxidil causes hirsutism (used topically for baldness) and diazoxide raises blood sugar (used in hypoglycaemia from insulinoma).
- **Hydralazine** causes reflex tachycardia and, on long use, a lupus-like syndrome in slow acetylators.

**Synthesis of methyldopate hydrochloride.** 1. **Vanillin**-derived or **3,4-dimethoxyphenylacetone** routes are used industrially; the classical teaching route starts from **3,4-dimethoxyphenylacetone**, which is converted by the **Strecker reaction** (sodium cyanide and ammonium chloride/ammonia) to the amino nitrile. 2. **Hydrolysis** of the nitrile with acid gives racemic 3-(3,4-dimethoxyphenyl)-2-methylalanine; the methyl ethers are cleaved with hydrogen iodide or hydrobromic acid to free the catechol, giving racemic methyldopa, and the **(S)-isomer is resolved** (only the levo form is active). 3. **Esterification** with ethanol saturated with dry hydrogen chloride gives the ethyl ester as its **hydrochloride**, which is freely water soluble and suitable for intravenous use.

## Remember

1. Organic nitrates are nitric acid **esters** (R—O—NO2); they release nitric oxide, raise cGMP and dilate veins more than arteries.
2. Nitrate tolerance is real: keep a daily nitrate-free interval. Never give a nitrate with sildenafil.
3. Dihydropyridines act on vessels, verapamil on the heart, diltiazem on both. The C4 aryl group must be perpendicular and *ortho/meta* substituted.
4. Diuretic sites: acetazolamide proximal, mannitol osmotic, furosemide thick ascending limb, thiazides distal tubule, spironolactone/amiloride collecting duct.
5. A free —SO2NH2 is essential for acetazolamide, thiazides and furosemide; substituting its nitrogen kills activity.
6. Thiazide SAR: sulphamoyl at 7, electron-withdrawing group at 6, saturated 3,4-bond for ten times the potency.
7. Loop diuretics lose calcium; thiazides keep it. Loop diuretics are ototoxic in high intravenous doses.
8. ACE inhibitors: zinc-binding group (SH, COOH, phosphinate); cough from bradykinin; most are ester prodrugs; avoid in pregnancy.
9. Methyldopa works through the false transmitter α-methylnoradrenaline and is the drug of choice in pregnancy; methyldopate is its soluble ester for injection.
10. Syntheses to write without hesitation: acetazolamide (thiadiazole → acetylate → sulphonyl chloride → ammonia), chlorothiazide (chlorosulphonation → ammonia → formic acid ring closure), furosemide (chlorosulphonation → ammonia → furfurylamine), methyldopate (Strecker → hydrolyse and demethylate → resolve → esterify).

# Unit 3: Antiarrhythmic, antihyperlipidaemic, coagulant and anticoagulant drugs, and drugs for heart failure

Four groups sit in this unit, all of them cardiovascular: drugs that correct the **rhythm** of the heart, drugs that lower **blood lipids**, drugs that help or hinder **clotting**, and drugs used in **congestive heart failure**. The starred drugs are **disopyramide phosphate** and **warfarin**.

## 3.1 The cardiac action potential and how antiarrhythmics work

A working cardiac cell has five phases. Phase 0 is the fast upstroke carried by **sodium** entering; phase 1 a brief repolarisation; phase 2 the plateau held up by **calcium** coming in; phase 3 repolarisation by **potassium** leaving; phase 4 the resting level, which in pacemaker cells drifts upward (the "funny" current) until threshold is reached.

```text
      1 ╭──╮ 2 (plateau, Ca2+ in)
        │   ╰─────────╮
   0 ▲  │              ╰╮ 3 (K+ out)
     │  │               ╰────────── 4 (rest / pacemaker drift)
  Na+ in
```

An arrhythmia arises either because an abnormal focus fires too fast or because an impulse circles round a ring of tissue (**re-entry**). Drugs act by slowing conduction, by lengthening the refractory period, or by suppressing abnormal automaticity. Note that every antiarrhythmic can itself provoke an arrhythmia — **pro-arrhythmia** is the great danger of this class.

### Vaughan Williams classification

| Class | Action | Drugs in the syllabus | Effect on the action potential |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IA | Moderate sodium block, also blocks potassium | Quinidine sulphate, procainamide hydrochloride, disopyramide phosphate* | Slows phase 0, lengthens the action potential and QT |
| IB | Weak sodium block, acts mainly on damaged tissue | Lidocaine hydrochloride, phenytoin sodium, tocainide hydrochloride, mexiletine hydrochloride | Shortens the action potential; little effect on normal cells |
| IC | Strong sodium block | Lorcainide hydrochloride (also flecainide, propafenone) | Markedly slows conduction, little change in duration |
| II | Beta blockers | Propranolol, esmolol, sotalol (also class III) | Slow the sinus node and AV conduction |
| III | Potassium channel block | Amiodarone, sotalol | Greatly lengthens the action potential and refractory period |
| IV | Calcium channel block | Verapamil, diltiazem | Slow the SA and AV nodes |

Points that examiners look for:

- **Quinidine**, a cinchona alkaloid and the dextro-isomer of quinine, also has antimuscarinic action, so it can speed AV conduction; it causes **cinchonism** (ringing in the ears, headache, blurred vision) and can lengthen the QT interval.
- **Procainamide** is the amide analogue of procaine: replacing the ester by an amide stops plasma esterases destroying it, so it is orally active and longer lasting. Long use produces a **lupus-like syndrome**, particularly in slow acetylators, because its metabolism depends on N-acetyltransferase.
- **Disopyramide** has the strongest antimuscarinic effect of the group (dry mouth, urinary retention) and the strongest negative effect on the force of contraction, so it is avoided in heart failure.
- **Lidocaine** is given only intravenously because of heavy first-pass metabolism; it is the traditional choice for ventricular arrhythmia after myocardial infarction.
- **Phenytoin** is useful mainly in arrhythmias caused by digitalis toxicity.
- **Amiodarone** is iodine-rich and very lipophilic, with a half-life of weeks; its toxicities are therefore organ-based — thyroid (both over- and underactivity), lung fibrosis, corneal deposits, skin discolouration and liver damage.
- **Sotalol** is a racemate: the *l*-isomer gives beta blockade (class II), while both isomers block potassium channels (class III).

### Synthesis of disopyramide phosphate

1. **Phenylacetonitrile** is treated with **sodium amide** and then with **2-chloropyridine** (or 2-bromopyridine). The carbanion displaces the halide and gives **α-phenyl-2-pyridylacetonitrile**.
2. A second deprotonation with sodium amide, followed by **2-(diisopropylamino)ethyl chloride**, alkylates the same carbon, giving 4-(diisopropylamino)-2-phenyl-2-(2-pyridyl)butanenitrile.
3. The nitrile is **partially hydrolysed with concentrated sulphuric acid** (stopping at the amide stage, not going on to the acid) to give **disopyramide**.
4. The base is neutralised with **phosphoric acid** to give the water-soluble **phosphate salt**.

## 3.2 Antihyperlipidaemic agents

Cholesterol and triglycerides travel in lipoproteins. **LDL** carries cholesterol to the tissues and is the harmful fraction; **HDL** carries it back to the liver and is protective. Lowering LDL slows atherosclerosis.

| Class | Drug | Mechanism | Points to note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fibrate | Clofibrate | Activates PPAR-α: more lipoprotein lipase, so triglycerides fall; HDL rises | Mainly for high triglycerides; causes gallstones and myopathy; largely replaced by newer fibrates |
| Statin | Lovastatin | Competitive inhibitor of **HMG-CoA reductase**, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis; liver LDL receptors increase, so plasma LDL falls | A fungal product; it is a **lactone prodrug** opened in the body to the active hydroxy acid; myopathy and raised transaminases are the risks |
| Bile acid sequestrants | Cholestyramine, colestipol | Insoluble anion-exchange resins that bind bile acids in the gut and prevent their reabsorption, so the liver uses cholesterol to make more | Not absorbed, so systemically safe; cause constipation and bind fat-soluble vitamins and other drugs — give other drugs an hour before or several hours after |

The lactone ring of lovastatin opens to a **3,5-dihydroxy acid** whose arrangement imitates the natural substrate HMG-CoA; this mimicry is the standard example of substrate-analogue design in this subject. Best taken at night, since cholesterol synthesis peaks then.

## 3.3 Coagulants and anticoagulants

**Clotting in one picture.** Both the contact (intrinsic) and tissue-factor (extrinsic) pathways converge on factor X; activated factor X turns prothrombin into thrombin, and thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin. Factors II, VII, IX and X need **vitamin K** for a post-translational step in the liver.

```text
Vitamin K (reduced) ──► γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X ──► vitamin K epoxide
          ▲                                                                │
          └────────── vitamin K epoxide reductase ◄───────────────────────┘
                              ✗ blocked by warfarin
```

### Coagulants (vitamin K compounds)

- **Menadione** (vitamin K3) is a synthetic naphthoquinone; it is water-insoluble but its sodium bisulphite adduct is soluble for injection. **Acetomenadione** (menadiol diacetate) is the diacetyl ester of the reduced form, used orally.
- Uses: bleeding from vitamin K deficiency, haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, obstructive jaundice and malabsorption, and reversal of excessive warfarin effect.
- Menadione can cause haemolysis and jaundice in newborns and in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, so phytomenadione (vitamin K1) is preferred in neonates.

### Oral anticoagulants

**Warfarin*** is a **4-hydroxycoumarin** with a 3-(1-phenyl-3-oxobutyl) side chain. It is the standard example of **bioisosterism with vitamin K** — the flat coumarin ring imitates the naphthoquinone, and so warfarin competitively inhibits **vitamin K epoxide reductase**. Because already-made clotting factors must be used up first, the effect begins only after 2–3 days, and warfarin is useless in an emergency. Features worth marks:

- Almost completely bound to albumin, so displacement (aspirin, sulphonamides, phenylbutazone) suddenly raises the free fraction.
- Metabolised by cytochrome P450; enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenobarbitone, carbamazepine) weaken it, inhibitors (cimetidine, metronidazole, fluconazole) strengthen it. Eating large amounts of green leafy vegetables also weakens it.
- Monitoring is by **prothrombin time, reported as INR**. The antidote is **vitamin K**, with fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex when bleeding is severe.
- It crosses the placenta and is teratogenic, so **heparin is used in pregnancy** instead.
- **Anisindione** is an indanedione anticoagulant acting by the same mechanism, now little used because of hypersensitivity reactions.
- **Clopidogrel** is not an anticoagulant but an **antiplatelet** drug: it is a thienopyridine prodrug activated by cytochrome P450 to a metabolite that irreversibly blocks the platelet **P2Y12 ADP receptor** for the platelet's lifetime. It is used after stenting, in acute coronary syndrome and in stroke prevention.

### Synthesis of warfarin

1. **4-Hydroxycoumarin** is prepared from a salicylate derivative: methyl salicylate (or o-hydroxyacetophenone) is cyclised with ethyl acetate / sodium, giving the 4-hydroxycoumarin ring with its active methylene-like C3 position.
2. **Benzylideneacetone** (4-phenyl-3-buten-2-one) is made by an aldol condensation of **benzaldehyde with acetone** followed by loss of water.
3. The two are combined in a base-catalysed **Michael addition**: C3 of 4-hydroxycoumarin adds across the double bond of benzylideneacetone, giving **warfarin**, which is used as the racemate although the (S)-isomer is several times more potent.

## 3.4 Drugs used in congestive heart failure

In heart failure the ventricle cannot pump enough blood; the body compensates with sympathetic drive and with salt and water retention, which eventually make matters worse. Treatment either strengthens the beat or unloads the heart.

### Cardiac glycosides

**Digoxin** and **digitoxin** come from *Digitalis* species. Each has a **steroid nucleus with a cis-trans-cis ring fusion, an unsaturated five-membered lactone ring at C17 (a cardenolide) and a sugar chain at C3**.

SAR in three lines:

1. The **lactone ring at C17 is essential** — opening or saturating it destroys activity.
2. The **14β-hydroxyl and the cis ring junctions** give the molecule its characteristic bent shape; flattening it abolishes activity.
3. The **sugars** are not needed for action but control water solubility, absorption, protein binding and duration. Digitoxin has one fewer hydroxyl than digoxin, so it is more lipophilic, better absorbed, far more protein bound and much longer acting.

**Mechanism:** the glycoside inhibits the **Na+/K+-ATPase** of the cardiac cell. Intracellular sodium rises, so the sodium-calcium exchanger works less, intracellular calcium rises and contraction becomes stronger (**positive inotropic effect**). Vagal stimulation also slows the AV node, which is why digoxin is used to control the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation.

**Toxicity** is common because the margin is narrow: anorexia, nausea and vomiting, yellow-green visual haloes, confusion, and arrhythmias of almost any kind. **Hypokalaemia** (often caused by a diuretic given at the same time) greatly increases toxicity, because potassium and the glycoside compete for the same site on the pump. Treatment is to stop the drug, correct potassium, give phenytoin or lidocaine for ventricular arrhythmia, and in severe cases digoxin-specific antibody fragments.

### Newer agents in the syllabus

- **Nesiritide** is recombinant human **B-type natriuretic peptide**. It raises cyclic GMP, dilates veins and arteries and promotes sodium loss; it is given by infusion in acutely decompensated heart failure. Being a peptide, it cannot be given orally.
- **Bosentan** is an orally active **endothelin receptor antagonist** (blocks ETA and ETB). Endothelin-1 is the body's strongest vasoconstrictor, so blocking it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance. Bosentan is used chiefly in **pulmonary arterial hypertension**; it is hepatotoxic and teratogenic, so liver tests and pregnancy prevention are mandatory.
- **Tezosentan** is a short-acting intravenous endothelin antagonist developed for acute heart failure.

Other classes used in heart failure, worth one line each: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (reduce afterload and remodelling), beta blockers in low slowly increased doses (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol), diuretics for congestion, and spironolactone for its survival benefit.

## Remember

1. Vaughan Williams: I sodium (A lengthens, B shortens, C little change), II beta blockers, III potassium, IV calcium.
2. Quinidine → cinchonism; procainamide → lupus-like syndrome; disopyramide → antimuscarinic and negative inotropic; amiodarone → thyroid, lung, cornea, skin.
3. Procainamide is the amide of procaine; the amide resists esterases, so it is orally active.
4. Statins are HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors; lovastatin is a lactone prodrug; the open 3,5-dihydroxy acid mimics HMG-CoA.
5. Resins bind bile acids in the gut, are not absorbed, and interfere with the absorption of other drugs and of fat-soluble vitamins.
6. Warfarin is a 4-hydroxycoumarin bioisostere of vitamin K; it blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, takes 2–3 days to act, is monitored by INR, is reversed by vitamin K, and is avoided in pregnancy.
7. Clopidogrel is a prodrug that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 receptor.
8. Cardiac glycoside SAR: C17 lactone essential, 14β-OH and cis ring fusion essential, sugars control pharmacokinetics only.
9. Digoxin inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase → calcium rises → stronger beat; hypokalaemia increases toxicity; yellow-green vision is the classic sign.
10. Syntheses to write without hesitation: disopyramide (phenylacetonitrile → 2-chloropyridine → aminoalkyl chloride → partial hydrolysis) and warfarin (4-hydroxycoumarin + benzylideneacetone, Michael addition).
